speechtext:
Yesterday in my absence from the house the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Jones) referred to the situation with regard to the smelt fishing season, particularly on the Restigouche river. I may tell my hon. friend that no extension of the smelt fishing season has been granted this year in Quebec or any other province. Of course the fisheries of the province of Quebec are administered by the provincial authorities, but the granting of an extension of any season is within the power of the federal government. We have not granted any such extension, and if any fishing is being carried on beyond the limits of the season it is being done illegally. At all events, we are making inquiries of the provincial government with regard to the real situation, and we will see if the officials are keeping on the job.

Mr. Speaker, with the unanimous consent of the house I would move that Bill No. 8 to amend the Trade Mark and Design Act be referred back to the committee of the whole.

Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Minister may refuse to register trade mark in certain eases.

This section sets forth
two additional reasons why the minister may refuse to register any trade mark or union label. The object, as I explained when the bill was before the committee previously, is to bring our act into line with the decisions made at The Hague conference, where it was decided that we should not grant trade marks which constituted a reproduction or imitation liable to create confusion with the trade mark of another unionist country. In subsection (f) the following words appear:

with a trade mark known to be the mark of a national of another country -
It has been represented to me that it would be better to have that more clearly defined, and that we should adopt the exact wording of the decision arrived at at The Hague. I therefore move that the words " known to be " be struck out and that there be substituted therefore the words " which is considered by the competent authority to be well known in Canada as ".

I am inclined to think that perhaps the sense of The Hague convention -would be better met by specifying the competent authority in this country. The words " competent authority " were used at The Hague in order to meet the requirements of all nations, but as each nation has its competent authority designated by statute, might it not be better to express in our act the name of the competent authority, which in this case I believe is a judge of the exchequer court.
Our competent authority under that section would be the commissioner.
Yes, subject to appeal.

Agriculture-for experiments in dehydration of fruits and vegetables, $10,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
When this estimate was before the committee a few days ago we were asked to let it stand. The committee will remember that I explained that the committee on dehydration had not been able to meet owing to the fact that three of its five members were absent from Canada. They convened only the day before yesterday. At that meeting they made a complete recommendation as to how this $10,000 could, in their estimation, be expended to the best advantage. Perhaps it would save time if I read their report:
Proposed Activities of Dehydration Committee 1928-1929
In the province of Nova Scotia, it is proposed at the experimental station, Kentville, there be installed a small dehydrator of cabinet type, to be used for research work in dehydration. Although this installation is for experimental purposes, yet it will have a capacity up to one and a half tons of apples per day, hence it is semi-commercial. Dehydration work with apples will be done this year, and a complete study of varieties commonly grown as to their suitability will be undertaken, and demonstration work with regard to the importance of grading of fruit previous to dehydration, and the grading of the dehydrated product. This plant will cost approximately $2,000 and the material and labour $3,000.
In the province of British Columbia the three-unit plant formerly operated at Penticton will be installed at the station at Summerland. This plant will be operated this year on apricots and prunes which will be available in the orchards in the Penticton and Summerland areas. The great importance of production of suitable varieties; the proper ripening of prunes preparatory to dehydration justifies the planting of a ten acre orchard at Summerland for further complete study and demonstration work as to profitable prune production for dehydration. The importance of apricot dehydration is illustrated by the fact that our importations into Canada are still great. Dehydration in Canada has not been started yet. The planting of young orchards is such that within five years there will be a large surplus of apricots not
Supply-Agriculture

required for the fresh fruit trade which of necessity will be dehydrated, thus replacing present importations.
In addition to the above, at Agassiz there will be conducted dehydration work in connection with loganberries. The cost of the work in British Columbia will be distributed about as follows:
Planting of demonstration prune and
apricot orchards	$ 1,200
Dehydration operations in apricots and prunes	3,000
Dehydration operations in loganberries	 800
We received information only yesterday from the government of British Columbia in reply to a communication of ours of about three weeks ago inquiring whether we could lease a five-acre plot of ground in the Oliver district for the purpose of planting this apricot orchard. The British Columbia government wired us that they would be pleased to lease us, at a nominal rental, five acres in that district for this purpose. The same kind of experimentation will be conducted at the Summerland experimental station with the idea of developing the best variety of fruit and ascertaining the stage of development at which it will dehydrate to the best advantage.
With regard to the situation in the maritime provinces, it will be recalled that in the absence of any such program as I have just outlined my sympathies were rather disposed to favour the improvement of the commercial plant in Annapolis valley. Neither Dr. Gris-dale nor I was able to give on the last occasion the name of the owner of that plant; it turns out that the establishment belongs to the United Fruit Growers. Inasmuch as neither of us had ever dealt with that case we were not in a position to give the name from memory. We have also learned that these growers have recovered very largely from their early disappointment and their plant is now in fairly good shape. Nevertheless they have not yet got into their stride, and the same applies to two other plrnts in the Annapolis valley. Consequently we have decided to set up a $5,000 dehydrating plant at Kentville for the purpose of testing out and demonstrating the best varieties of fruit for dehydration.
There is a tendency to use any kind of fruit for dehydration; anything that is unsuitable for the fresh fruit trade, it is considered, is good enough for the dehydration plant. That is a fallacy; it will not work. It has been found many times that ycu cannot convert poor fresh fruit into a good dehydrated product. A reasonable standard of quality must be maintained in the raw fruit if the converted commodity is to be of good
	-
quality. Size, quality and many other factors in relation to dehydration will be investigated at the Kentville station along the same lines as have been pursued in the Kelowna valley during the past four years. I have i report, copies of which may be obtained on application, of the work that has been carried on during the four years that this vote has appeared in the estimates, the present being the fifth occasion on which the grant is being made. It might curtail the discussion somewhat if I read this report, which is quite interesting. Here are the conclusions:
The results of these investigations might be briefly summarized as follows:
(1)	' It is impossible for a dehydrator to make a good product from low-grade fresh fruit.
As will be noted from the passage I have quoted, it is essential that a reasonably good raw fruit be used if a good product is to be obtained.
(2)	The hope for permanency and prosperity in the Canadian dried-fruit industry lies in creating a greater confidence therein by both the domestic and foreign trade, and by emphasizing high quality. This can be done perhaps more effectively through dehydraters than through the evaporators. A reduction in costs is equally important. The dehydrater, once established, can operate at a lower cost per ton of dried fruit than the evaporator.
The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie) brought up this matter last year when h& inquired as to the relative cost of dehydration and evaporation. The conclusion arrived at after four years of investigation is that the dehydrating plant once established can operate at a lower cost per ton than the evaporator, and, of course, the product is much more acceptable to the purchasing public.
3. The fruit-growers themselves must carefully consider the matter of their plantations in relationship to dehydration. It is impossible to expect a trade to be developed on an insecure supply of a large number of varieties. Hence, our fruit plantations must be somewhat remodelled with that end in view.
The trouble in the past has been that a good many people have looked upon dehydrated fruit as a by-product, something that has been made fairly presentable from a poor raw material. That idea is altogether erroneous. The conclusion in this regard is this:
(4)	Dehydrated fruit must be considered a fruit product and not a mere by-product.
(5)	It would be wise for those considering plantations for dehydration purposes to consider carefully the relationship between the dried-fruit industry and other phases of the fruit industry. Often the dehydration plant should

Supply-Agriculture
either be operated under the same company, or in close co-operation with the fresh-fruit warehouses. the canning plants, cider plants, cider and fruit-juice plants, jam, jelly, and marmalade plants.
That is obvious. The cost of administration would be reduced if all the operating units were centralized.
(6)	There still remains considerable work to be done thoroughly to classify the suitability of uniformly good grades of the different varieties of our various fruits and vegetables.
The foregoing are -the conclusions arrived at in this report covering the experimental work carried on over the last four years.

Why is it necessary to
grow apricots in British Columbia when, as the minister says, in three or four years' time there will be far more apricots in the district than there will be a market for? Why do we need to grow more?

Some varieties will
dehydrate better than others and the department is leasing five acres from the provincial government, very much to their satisfaction, for the purpose of testing these varieties.

How long will it take
to produce fruit if you plant to-day?

The sooner you
begin the sooner you get fruit.

That is self-evident, but
it does not tell us how long it takes to produce apricots.
Five or six years.
That is to say, it will be six years before you make the tests and you are putting in your dehydrating plant now?

There were
orchards planted immediately after the war and they are bearing now.
I know that.

But they were
planted indiscriminately as to quality and suitability for dehydration. They are bearing now and we shall be able to make tests with these while the other trees are growing. The result will be a continuous supply of new raw material for experimental purposes. If there were no trees bearing now the hon. gentleman's criticism would be warranted, but there is a substantial number of trees, although I am unable to say precisely how many thousands. It is a large soldier settlement where fruit-growing, particularly the producing of apricots, was undertaken after
the war. The soldiers found the undertaking somewhat onerous and this is one way in which we can help them to improve the quality of their product and enable them to compete in any market.

The minister thinks I
am criticising him. I was merely asking him for information, and he certainly has not given us a clear explanation of what he is doing. He says he is planting trees with the idea of finding out in the future which are the best varieties to grow. He also advises us that it will take six years to determine from the trees we are now planting what quality of fruit they will produce. He is putting in a dehydrating plant at once to test the kind of fruit which will be produced six years from now. That may not be what he said but it is the effect of his remarks. Can he not find out, by testing the fruit which is now being produced, what are the most suitable varieties? That is the common sense of the matter, and I know something about it because I come from a fruit district.
We are not putting in a dehydrating plant at Oliver and I did not say that we were. We are transferring the plant that has been at Penticton.

Where are you putting
it?

We are transferring it to the experimental farm at Summer-land about eight miles from Oliver. There is no dehydrating plant at Oliver, which is simply an experimental orchard. In the meantime there will be an abundance of apricots to experiment with.

Is this work carried on
under the fruit branch or under some other department?
The fruit commissioner is on the committee, also Professor Macoun, Mr. Archibald, the director of experimental farms, Mr. McGillivray, Mr. McIntosh and Dr. Shutt.
Is this connected with the health of animals branch?
No, it comes under fruit.	.
What variety of prune has the' department found to be the most satisfactory for dehydration?

We have not done much of that as yet. It is for that purpose that we are establishing the plant at Sum-merland. We have a new orchard of ten
Supply-Agriculture

acres where we shall experiment particularly with prunes. There are very few varieties of prunes that have been dehydrated, but an enormous quantity of prune's comes into Canada, and we might just as well produce that article ourselves. There is no doubt that they can be grown, but it has not yet been demonstrated which is the best variety or what is the proper stage of maturity for dehydration. That will be established at Sum-merland.
We grow the Italian prune to perfection in many parts df British Columbia, and I was just wondering if that variety was satisfactory for dehydration purposes.
I understand it is.

What information has the minister with regard to the dehydration of the loganberry? That is a berry that is grown in great profusion. It is a fertile and a very profitable crop produced in many parts of British Columbia, particularly in the coast section and down on Vancouver island. We are already making most excellent wine from loganberries which after three or four years is equal in palatability, and also in pressure, to anything else. If we can find a new outlet for the loganberry, it will prove to be a very profitable crop for the growers in that section of the province.

My hon. friend is quite right; it has become quite a crop. In the summary from which I have just quoted there is a short paragraph with regard to loganberries which says that in addition to the work at Agassiz there will be conducted dehydration work in connection with loganberries. Here is a paragraph with regard to loganberries in the report covering the last four years:
Loganberries dehydrate into a delightful product. The colour, flavour and appearance are well preserved. When dehydrated they are almost as natural in appearance as the fresh fruit.
I might add that whereas the loss of weight in most evaporated fruits amounts to approximately twenty per cent, in the case of the loganberry moisture is absorbed in sufficient quantity to restore the fruit almost to its original weight as well as to its original quality. '

I think the minister is to be congratulated in carrying on this work of dehydration of various fruits in the Okanagan valley. The experimental plant which has been in operation there for three years has arrived at some very valuable findings which have recently been published.

W ith regard to one clause in that report it is particularly worth noting that as the grading of apples has got better and better, the quality of the cull apples left behind has also improved. Whilst dehydration is of very little use economically for the small under-sized crooked apples, the better the quality of the culls, the more culls there are in a hundred pounds which can lend themselves to dehydration. As a practical result of these experiments at Penticton, a small dehydration plant has successfully been started at Vernon on a commercial basis, and the minister has a sample of the dehydrated apples which they are putting on the market. To my mind the greatest future before these experiments lies in the dehydration of prunes, largely because Canada imports an enormous quantity of prunes every year. Throughout the Okanagan valley, and especially the southern part of it, prunes have been grown very successfully for the last twenty years. The Italian prune is the most popular variety, but it remains to be seen whether the Italian prune will prove as good for dehydration purposes as other varieties of prunes, and one of the values that I attach to this lease of land from the provincial government at Oliver is that there it will be demonstrated whether Italian prunes are the most likely to produce the maximum of results from dehydration. I do not know just where that five acres is situated, but I have no doubt that on it there will be growing already apricots, and very probably apples. Is not that so?
Nothing as yet.

Undoubtedly apricots and apples, and I should imagine prunes, are being grown on the neighbouring land, and that will be an extremely good basis from which to start. I also agree with the moving of the dehydration plant from Penticton to the experimental farm at Summerland. That is a wise piece of business. It brings one more piece of work under the minister in that neighbourhood, directly under the eye and supervision of his representative at the farm. I think the fruit growing interests of British Columbia will be well served if the experiment is carried on along the lines the minister suggests.

Has the
minister considered the advisability of establishing a plant in the Niagara peninsula for the dehydration of fruit-apples and other products-or has such a plant been established there?

Supply-Agriculture

Some years ago
-before my time at least-dehydration was established at Grimsby right in the heart of the fruit country, but at that time they still held to the old idea that anything at all would do to dehydrate. The result was it was never satisfactory. They did not seem to take to the idea. It was a fresh fruit country, and although the establishment was a good one, and although an artificial ice production plant was constructed for the purpose of icing the cars, they never made use of it and are not using it now. They are using the ice plant to ice cars when required, and also to create a sheet of hockey ice in the adjoining rink.

Is there a
market for this particular product of dehydrated fruit?

Yes, a very large
market; but a great many people do not seem to differentiate between dehydrated and evaporated fruit. Some of the enthusiasts who first advocated dehydration left the impression that anything would do. Then when it was tried it did not produce a good product and did not take on the market. But they are getting over that idea now. There is a commercial plant at Kelowna, and another one at Vernon. I do not know whether the hon. member knows of any more or not. I think they are doing well. In the maritimes there are three plants which are doing fairly well, but not nearly as well as if they had an experimental plant in their midst, to give them the same advantage as the Kelowna plant got -at Penticton, and that is the reason we are establishing one at Kentville.

I see that covers them all. I presume my
hon. friend wants to know what this increase is to be used for. The house will recall that in addition to taking care of the general growth of this system it was hoped we would be able to make an extension last year or this year to some one or two of these farms. That is the one at Lethbridge, the central farm here. The equipment was getting inadequate to meet the situation. The other was the new tobacco farm at L'Assomption. We found the money grant was not sufficiently generous to take care of the central farm enlargement; so that it was spent on the Lethbridge farm and the new tobacco station at L'Assomption. This year we have been trying to arrange for an extension to the central farm. We have been negotiating for some time, but owing to the difference between the price asked by t'he owner of the property, and what we think we could afford to give, no transaction has as yet been consummated. There were three in prospect last year, and we have three in prospect this year. We will take up such one as the vote will permit our purchasing and we can make the best arrangements for. As the years pass by the valley of the Assiniboine is flooded with greater frequency than in the early days, with the result that a very large part of the Brandon experimental farm is inundated about every third year; that has occurred at least two or three times since I took charge of the department. Consequently we require an extension of that farm. A small extension at the Agassiz farm is also required. Which of

these three we will use the vote for I do not know at this stage. It will depend upon how good a bargain we can make and how much money we have at our disposal. We are in hopes of getting an extension of the central farm here. Our persistency in this direction has not resulted in very much progress so far, notwithstanding the urgency of the case.
Cannot you expropriate?

It will be observed that part of this vote will cover the necessary buildings. In former years these had to appear in the Public Works estimates. It was thought to be more convenient to have this part of the expenditure included in uur vote for administration purposes. Consequently $50,000 will be so expended, and will not appear, as formerly, in the public works vote. So the increase will be that much less than appears on the surface.
What is the necessity for the increase of the central experimental farm? Is it going to be made into a beauty spot, or is it to be used for experimental purposes?

That question is very well put. It is already a beauty spot. I think great credit is due to the late Dr. Saunders for the way in which he laid out this farm forty years ago. At that time it was considered to be a good large farm, for it comprised about 460 acres. But to-day we are endeavouring to carry on our farming operations without sufficient land. Nearly every branch and provincial farm has been getting larger to meet the growing requirements of the country, but this farm has actually been growing smaller and smaller each decade so far as its utilization for practical purposes is concerned. The arboretum to the north of the Prescott highway takes up 62 acres; the shelter belt takes up 16 acres; the campus covers 13 acres; the orchard 40 acres; the experimental plots, the poultry runs and the paddocks and yards for the various branches of live stock take up a large acreage. The result is that for farming purposes the area is reduced to three fields of 40 acres each-120 acres. The campus of the Saskatoon university farm is twice as large as our campus. So cramped' have we been for space that during the meeting of the world's poultry congress here last August we had to use our wits to conceal the lack of pasturage for our chickens. We did the best we could-we put some of our chickens on a piece of tillable land, and about 1,300 others we sent out to a private farm. The year before we put our 
chickens out on the rifle range, where we lost about a thousand dollars' worth due to the unsuitable nature of the ground. When an experimental farm in the very heart and nerve centre of the Dominion has not enough land to pasture its chickens, it seems to me we had better give up farming altogether or get additional acreage. But a far more serious question arises with respect to our young cattle. We send them out to the same rifle ranges, and I do not know what we should do but for the good nature of the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), who lets us have the land at a nominal rental. Then we have 65 head of milch cows of various breeds to look after. We have no pasture for them. Last year we fenced off temporarily five or six acres of new meadow land that had been seeded down the year previous. In wet weather it does not take 65 cattle long to make such a small enclosure look more like a corral in the west than pastureland. In the summer time those cows are housed all through the day. At five o'clock in the evening we let them out to have their little frolic in this five-acre plot of nominal pasture, then at five o'clock in the morning they are brought in for their breakfast and kept in for another twelve hours. That practice has been going on for ten or fifteen years. Well now, it seems to me it is about time we provided a little real pastureland for those " critters." When Premier Bruce and Premier Coates were here last winter I was thankful it was that season of the year, because both of them are practical farmers. Premier Coates was more interested in live stock, and when I have a practical man like that to show around I have to keep dodging to prevent his getting to know too much about the weaknesses of our layout.

You can do it all
right.

That is not a joke, it is a fact. As I think everybody knows, the original owner of about 100 acres of the present central farm was the late J. R. Booth. He was an old resident and we all recognized the sentimental value he placed upon the Booth farm-he held it away up at $1,500 an acre. Of course he did not want to sell, and I could not blame him, for he was associated with the place for the best part of his life. Now, however, the present owners are prepared to talk business, although their price is still too high. I feel very strongly that we should not continue any longer with our present cramped quarters if we are to have a real central farm. It must be remem-

Supply-Agriculture
bered that this is the centre of our whole system of experimental farms. It is here that we develop new wheats. During the last few years we have, in a small way, grown the wheat under glass in the winter, and so reduced by half the time required to develop a new variety; but with only sufficient room to do it on a single plot instead of a triplicate plot system, and with very little glass for continuing this experimental work through the winter, it takes us a little better than double the usual time to develop a new wheat. It seems to me that since Canada is developing in this way, with at least half of the people engaged in agriculture, we can afford to have one farm here as the centre of the system, of a size commensurate with the importance and the innumerable requirements of agriculture.

Since one of these experimental farms is close to my own home, and since I am possibly responsible for a small part of the increase, perhaps it would not be amiss if I were to say something on this subject. Within recent years three important events have occurred in conncetion with that farm, the first being the magnificent donation of Mr. W. R. Patterson, which was mentioned in the house last year. Mr. Patterson owned 640 acres of land immediately north of the experimental farm, one of the finest farms in western Canada, with a fine spring, good buildings and the land in a good state of cultivation, and he has given this as an addition to the present farm. Nominally I suppose this farm is being held by the government at a small rental, but evenutally it is to become the absolute property of the Dominion of Canada.
The next event, and a rather happy one, was a hail storm. I had been trying for a year or more to persuade the Minister of Agriculture that a new greenhouse was required on that farm, since the one then existing was a small building erected in 1888, which had become a fine illustration of decay. The minister was visiting in the west, and while he was there I prayed for a hail storm, which eventually came and finished the greenhouse. I then telephoned the minister asking him to pay a visit to the farm, which he kindly consented to do, and I knew that would settle the matter. It did; the greenhouse is already built and is a credit to the farm.
The third matter which I desired to mention was in connection with the horse breed-ng business. For some years, under the able management of the superintendent, Mr. W. H. Gibson, they have been engaged in breeding Clydesdale horses, and have produced some
of the best Clydesdales in Canada. Last fall a number of these horses were exhibited at Toronto, but for a reason easy to explain they did not succeed very well at that exhibition. The same horses were taken to Chicago, however, where they were awarded a number of the very best prizes in competition with the rest of the North American continent, and as I understand it, one of these horses was awarded the title of the best Clydesdale mare in North America. A Scotch judge, who was judging some of these horses at Toronto, said about one horse that he would like to take it back to Scotland with him. I think that shows that we have made great advances in Canada in this connection. Of course all the provinces do not specialize in the same breeds, but I fancy that within the next ten or fifteen years western Canada may become the source of supply of the very best Clydesdales, and we will find breeders coming to Canada from the LTnited States and perhaps even from Scotland to buy their stock. Therefore I wish to commend the minister on the management of this farm at Indian Head.

Before anyone
else speaks I would like to refer for a moment to Mr. Patterson's donation of a whole section of land, fully equipped with the exception of machinery. I have known that farm ever since it was homesteaded, and it is a wonderful property. We had an experimental farm there consisting of 680 acres; Mr. Patterson knew the government required more land, and he contributed another 640 acres, feeling that his original homestead could not be put to a better use. He has been living there right beside the experimental farm for nearly forty years, and he appreciated the work done. We have to get up some speed or private interests will step in and do work which naturally falls to the lot of the government. It is no secret that when our research experts were taken from Winnipeg to Australia and to Toronto, the wheat pool offered to make up an addition to their salaries sufficient to keep them here. We should not have that condition; surely we should speed up, and not only extend our farms but also pay our men salaries sufficiently adequate so that they will not gravitate away to other countries when they receive better offers. I am sure that when the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) knows all the facts in connection with this farm, his judgment will tell him that we must either go forward or go back, and this is not the time to go back. The more the west grows the more tremendous are the problems to be solved in connection with cereal culture. This year our loss from rust

is estimated to be at least a hundred million dollars, and my opinion is that it will be a great deal more. In addition to that matter, our experimental farms are taking up the question of root rots and a number of other important things, so it will be seen that we will be doing a real work. Perhaps when the rust laboratory at the farm gets started we may have all this work under one administration, although I doubt if that can be done because you have to operate right in the rust field. I should like to ask the
Minister of Agriculture three questions: first, what portion of the appropriation of $1,900,000 for experimental farms goes to British Columbia; secondly, what part of the total appropriation is to be applied to the erection of new buildings; thirdly, is it the intention of the govex-nment to extend the operation of experimental farms and give one to the great area of central British Columbia?

While my deputy
is looking up the desired information with regard to my hon. friend's first question I will answer his third. I was in hopes some years ago of being able to carry out the expectations of my predecessor in establishing a new experimental farm up in the Prince Rupert district between Fort George and Rupert, and made a trip through that country in order to judge of its character. It holds out many advantages from an agricultural standpoint, but I found that the district was so inadequately equipped for the purpose that I concluded it would be better to improve existing farms to a reasonable degree, than to
establish new farms. There is a tremendous demand for the starting of new farms-I do not think there has been any less pressure in the case of this government as compared with preceding governments in that respect- but the most sensible proceeding would seem to be to complete the existing experimental farms and equip them properly. We have been starting a number of demonstration plots, and I think they have been doing pretty good work. Of course some people are very ambitious and would not for a moment look at little demonstration plots or small farms; they want big farms, equipped with buildings, and cattle, and other- kinds of live stock. Personally I think we have as many farms as we can afford to administer until a larger appropriation is voted, and that in some of the provinces we could do with fewer farms at this stage. But they are in existence, and hon. gentlemen will remember the old saying: Once a capital always a capital; once a farm always a farm, because it is pretty hard to let it go. In some of the provinces where there are many farms, four or five, the provincial governments have started negotiations with the department here looking towards the taking over of some of these farms for provincial purposes. Whether anything will come of it I do not know, but I look favourably on the proposal where a province has four or five farms. These farms have done excellent pioneer work and some of the provinces are desirous of taking over farms here and there. I am not going to say what purposes they have in view, but I may observe that they have been looking into the work carried on at the Alberta farm and have been looking into the schools, having in mind perhaps the possibility of establishing some primary agricultural farms such as were set up in Alberta some years ago. If we can make a business arrangement with them we may relinquish some of the farms and then extend into frontier areas. I am not going to make any promise in that regard but I should like to see something done in that direction. In the meantime we are doing what we can to establish the work on a sound basis, equipping old farms where necessary. To get the most satisfactory results we should really, if I may use the term, jack up the vote half a million every year, because we have been going along very niggardly. I may say that we are not going to come out square this year. As every farmer knows, the last two years have been exceedingly expensive in agriculture; and as costs have increased in the case of the private

farmer, where the harvesting is done in bad weather, so have they increased to the government, with the result that we are running somewhat behind. The total for British Columbia is $200,000. There are the Sidney farm on the island, Agassiz on the mainland, and Summerland and Invermere, besides some, substations in the north.

With regard to these experimental farms and the proposed enlargement of the central experimental farm at Ottawa, I quite agree that there is a marked necessity for the addition of certain lands to the central experimental farm. As far as the purchase of the lands is concerned, the best lands should be procured for lhe least possible money, always seeing to it they are well fitted for the purpose of which they are required. It is a very difficult matter of course to set any actual value on farm lands that are used for experimental purposes, where a great deal of the work that is carried on in the different lines is done on plots of one-fortieth of an acre. But it is common knowledge that the discoveries on this single farm at Ottawa have already yielded a revenue to the agriculture of this country that has amply paid for every dollar that has been expended on experimental farms or will be expended in that direction for some years to come. If these experiments are to be of value to the average farmer they must be carried on under ordinary farming conditions, that is, with a sufficient area to supply pasturage and the other things that one usually finds in connection with an ordinary mixed farm in Canada. So I should say that the purchase of these lands is an absolute necessity. The people of Canada are to be congratulated upon possessing the most complete system of experimental farms to be found in any other country, without a single exception. Those farms have developed; they have done a great deal of very valuable work for this .	56103-37
country, and properly conducted they have a great future. It would be a mistake, in my opinion, to cramp the central experimental farm at Ottawa, which is the one generally visited by agriculturists and others coming here from other parts of the world. Canada is too big a country to take any such narrow view of the situation.
Referring to what the hon. member for Skeena has said, I quite agree with his remarks in connection with the necessity for a farm in that huge inland empire known as central and northern British Columbia. British Columbia has an area larger than the three states to the south, an area greater than France and Italy and Switzerland oombined; so you can readily see that with one or two experimental farms located in the southern part of the country, where the conditions are entirely different from those that prevail in the north, it is impossible to obtain the best results and to give information that will be of value to those who are living in the northern section. That northern country is a great lake area, with rich lands, lightly timbered, and with many lakes and rivers. It is an ideal dairy country, with such a rainfall that you can have a stand of grass all summer. During the past year British Columbia was one huge field of grass wherever grass could grow, from the forty-ninth parallel to the Alaska boundary. Hon. members may be surprised to know that in British Columbia we have no less than 160,000,000 acres of range land, of which 100,000,000 acres are timbered and 60,000,000 open. To show you how slowly we are progressing, in one single year it has been found necessary for us to import seventy-five per cent of the meat we buy in British Columbia, running into a matter of 85,750,000, as well as 24,000 head of cattle, 63,000 sheep-as many as we have in the province-5,000 calves, and 113,000 hogs. That is the amount we imported into a country which has rich agricultural possibilities but is still in an undeveloped state. We are using but six per cent of our range land, while the state of Washington to the south is using about 69.7 per cent. Washington is not only feeding herself but is exporting her surplus products to other countries, and that shows how necessary it is to encourage the settlement of those great areas. I do not know anything that would give more encouragement to those farmers than a recognition on the part of this government, by the establishment of a suitable farm in that particular section, of the agricultural possibilities of the part of the country to which I refer.

During the time I had the honour to be Minister of Agriculture we decided to have a farm located in that section, after we had made a very thorough examination, and received reports from the experts of the Department of Agriculture connected with the experimental farm system. They reported favourably, and we would have established a farm there had it not been for the action of the Liberal party in defeating us at the next election. However, we have strongly urged this on the present Minister of Agriculture, and I feel sure that he could not dispose to better advantage of any of that surplus which the Minister of Finance mentioned yesterday in his budget speech than by immediately taking up this matter and establishing an experimental farm in that section. During my time as minister we established an experimental farm at Swift Current. A good many of the people were opposed to it at the time, but I understand that it is now rendering very excellent service to the farmers in that particular area. I have listened with
sympathetic interest to the statement made by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Brady), I believe that the work done by the experimental farm has proved to be of so much value to the farming interests of this country that the minister should take under consideration as soon as possible the extension of that system to a part of the country which is so badly in need of it. I am driven to that conclusion by my personal knowledge of the good work that has been done by the district farms. While speaking of this matter may I refer to the statement of the minister a moment ago that we were familiar with the system and with the probable changes. I quite agree with him, but I say that it is not so much that the problems are becoming more difficult or less difficult of solution, but they are becoming different. The pioneer days in the old parts of the provinces immediately in the vicinity of the experimental farms have gone. With 
them the pioneers problems have gone, but we are confronted day by day with changed problems that require new methods; the discovery of those new methods with accuracy and knowledge requires further experimentation, and I believe that it will be many years, if ever, before the time comes when we can do without our experimental farms. We have stressed in this house, and stressed rightly, the value of scientific research as applied to industry. It is my impression, and I think it is an impression which is shared by all those who have any knowledge of the subject whatever, that there is no occupation which more definitely requires the application of scientific information, which more definitely calls for further scientific research than that very occupation of agriculture. Dealing as we do, as every farmer must do, with nature itself, facing the varying climatic and soil conditions, and working as it were in the very laboratory of nature itself, it seems to me that there should be brought to the assistance of that occupation all the knowledge which can be obtained on the subject. I am perhaps more intimately acquainted with the experimental farm at Lacombe. I no longer represent that particular district, but my interests are the same as they were previously. I have spoken on the subject before. May I say again that I would be very sorry at any time to see a diminution of the interest taken in this matter, and I would be glad at any time to welcome an increase in the attention paid to those farms. They have done excellent work, as far as I have seen in my experience, and I think the money spent on these farms has been well expended. It is not merely a matter of discovering new seed varieties, or discovering the best method of caring for stock. There is another aspect to which I have referred before, and to which I shall refer again, and that is the protective effect. I do not see the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) in his place, but I know that he takes strong exception to the word "protection." But there is one form of protection with which I am in favour, and that is protection against the exploitation of the people of this country, and these farms are one of the best means of preventing the exploitation of farmers by unscrupulous men who at all times of the year come forward trying to sell some particular kind of seed which they say is of great value, which turns out to be of no value. The farmer is not in a position to experiment with these seeds. It would be ruinous for him to attempt to do so. His time is too precious. The work of the farms is experimental not commercial work,

and I disagree with those gentlemen who speak without knowledge, who say that the experimental farms should be self-supporting. That is not the purposes of these farms. The idea is that these farms Should carry on experimental work, such as no individual farmer can do. In that way we would increase the productiveness of the farm and the profits to the farmer. I am a farmer myself, but I think we in this house all realize that any grant which will assist better production in any line of business and lower production costs, or which will increase or improve the value and variety of products and will improve the possibilities of selling any product in the country, will be money well spent.
Again I urge upon the minister that he give his full support to these farms; in fact I know he will, and this house is more and more realizing that point, and will not only grant, without undue criticism, but will welcome the appropriation of money for additional expenditures when it can be proved that the result will be beneficial, and that the money will be spent in the most economical and efficient manner.
I should like to refer to what was said by the hon. member for Skeena in connection with agricultural training for young men. That work is carried on to a limited degree, it is true, in Alberta, but I may suggest to the hon. member that it was carried on by the provincial government. They endeavoured to train young men and young women, to give them a more scientific knowledge of the greatest occupation in the world -and I believe it is the greatest-and to elevate that occupation in their minds, so that their mental concept of farming should not be that of a servile occupation but that they should be imbued with the idea that agriculture in its proper sense is one of the greatest and most useful occupations in the world.

Mr. Chairman, I
should like to put in a word of appreciation

I think they had the industry; they worked hard enough, but conditions were such that success was almost impossible.	As the minister
knows, under present methods it costs from $100 to $500 an acre to clear land, and it is a question whether the land when cleared is worth that high figure.	If we can only
devise some new method of getting rid of these ancient stumps there will be a great deal of land put under cultivation which is capable of producing fruits and vegetables as well as grains, and about everything else that is grown anywhere outside of the tropical regions. There is an immense area in the Fraser valley which should be made available for agricultural purposes. I think possibly I represent the finest agricultural district in the whole of British Columbia, and that means a
Supply-Agriculture

good deal. I am sure I am safe in saying that I represent more farmers than any other member from British Columbia, and I would impress upon the minister the necessity for making some intensive study of the best method of clearing up our lands.

As my hon. friend
has raised not a new question but one new this afternoon, I think I will be justified in making some comment in that connection. We have figures because we have cleared up some of these lands in British Columbia, for instance at Sidney, but I hesitate to give the information to my hon. friend because I am afraid it would not be very conducive to immigration; the clearing of the land would cost too much. The situation is just the same as it was with the farmers in Ontario a hundred years ago. If the people of that time had known how much it was going to cost in money and labour to clear the land they might have hesitated about tackling it. Nevertheless they did tackle it and once they got interested they forgot all about the cost. They had more in the way of strong arms and healthy bodies than they had cash in the bank, and they kept working away until they cleared the land. That is the only course to follow in the case of these British Columbia lands that I know of. If you want to charge up the cost of clearing that land you must bear these facts in mind: You have to blow the whole thing to pieces with dynamite, and then as a consequenc of turning the under soil over on to your top soil you have to use fertilizer-the whole cost is a serious deterrent to settlement. Of course in the case of a man who wants to go in and make a home for himself regardless of the cost it is a different matter; but if he sits down, as a man should do when he wishes to build a house, and considers the cost he will never start it. This statement, of course, is not very encouraging.

That hardly answers
my question.

I do not care to
give the figures. It is very expensive if you charge up everything. But if you are really desirous of building a home, and you like the climate, and you clean up a little bit every year and have good health, you will get a good farm by the time you are ready to pass away.

Of course you will
have a good farm, but the minister has not dealt with my question at all.

Do you want me
to give the exact figures?

I am not asking for
figures. What I am asking is this: Is the department conducting any experiments as to the best and most economical method of clearing lands? The minister throws up his hands and says that the only way to clear lands is to get in and take out stumps- that is, follow the strong arm method; but sometimes it has been possible to use brains as well as strong arms. The question I am asking is: Has the minister access to brains, and is his department doing anything to investigate this particular matter?

Not for publication purposes. We are not only investigating but we are doing the actual work and know the actual cost. There has been some experimental work done, but primarily for clearing the land in Agassiz. A large part of that land is mountainous, and of 1,300 acres possibly only about 300 acres are tillable. The rest is so mountainous we could not convert it into arable land. There is some work being done in the direction my hon. friend suggests but it does not require experimenting. I do not see any particular advantage in finding the cost. The proper method to follow in a case of that kind is to take the timber off the land and commercialize it to the best advantage, apply it to whatever purposes it is most suitable for, and then blow out the stumps with dynamite. By so doing, however, you create big holes so that you would think you were in some shell-scarred region in France or Flanders. It is very expensive land to clear, because it i3 so heavily timbered, and then one has to use fertilizers, thereon in order to bring it into proper condition for production. We can give the desired information, but it would not be conducive to promoting the settlement of these timbered lands, which after all make expensive farm lands unless all the timber thereon can be used commercially.

I do not think the Minister of Agriculture is treating the hon. member quite fairly in refusing to answer the question on the ground that it may not conduce to furthering the immigration plans of the government. No greater condemnation of immigration plans with respect to British Columbia has been made in this house than the one uttered by the minister when he intimates that not only would labour extending over years be involved in clearing out a farm, but that the man would probably be in his grave before he had succeeded in getting a farm. I do not see why the information cannot be given.

Supply-Agriculture
I will give it to my hon. friend, but I do not think it will serve any good purpose. The land at Sidney is heavily timbered, and in some places the cost would be $500 an acre.

I wish to ask the minister for some figures that may not be quite so horrifying. How much of this item is to be devoted to increasing the area of the experimental farm in this city? I believe that farm is entirely too small. It is carrying on work which, it must be admitted, is in the interest of all the other experimental farms in Canada.
That is it.
And the area is entirely too small, in my judgment.
Hear, hear.

I do not know whether or not my information is correct, but I have been told that there is one block of land adjacent to the farm, of about 200 acres I think, which is being held at $600 per acre, and that the government is negotiating for the purchase of this particular block. I have also been informed that there is another farm, also close to the experimental farm, and of about the size and the same character of soil, which can be obtained for $200 an acre. I do not know whether or not these rumours are well founded, but I do think that the area of the farm here should be increased. Of course if the land can be obtained for $200 per acre it would be foolish to buy it for $600, even though some warm personal friend owned it. I have had the privilege of visiting pretty nearly all the experimental farms throughout the Dominion, and I believe they are doing a good work. I believe also that the work can be improved, and doubtless will be in years to come, as, under proper guidance, these farms make use of advanced scientific methods. Again let me remind hon. members of the house who advocate experimental farms or stations for their own particular district or province not to lose sight of the special scientific work, chemical and otherwise, which is being carried on here at Ottawa and under very cramped conditions.

In reply to my hon. friend I may say that Mr. Booth is asking $600 an acre for 321 acres, which will amount roughly to $190,000, but I am disposed to think further in the matter before acting. Not but what the land is worth the amount asked.
but in order to afford satisfaction to all parties, especially the taxpayers, I think the matter should be submitted to the exchequer court in order to get a valuation.
By expropriation?

Yes. We have
prices on three or four areas adjoining the Booth farm, submitted by the owners, and these will constitute, I presume, a basis for valuation if it is necessary to take the matter to the courts. We have tried to get a satisfactory adjustment with Mr. Booth, but before I should feel justified in paying $600 I think the fair thing to do would be to refer the question to the exchequer court.

What about asking prices on the other farms?
Mr. M'OTHERWELL: They run from $300 to $450.
How do they compare as regards suitability?
Some of them are excellent, but they do not begin to compare with the Booth farm for proximity, convenience and general suitability.

You have
some pretty good land in the experimental farm as it now stands. I do not know, but it seems to me that it might be worth considering whether in an experimental farm you should get the very best soil on the face of the earth or whether, on the contrary, it would not be advisable sometimes to carry on your experiments on average soil.
That is what the Booth farm is.
If the Booth farm is average then the others are under average.

The Caldwell farm, between the two highways, is on the whole heavier and more productive land; it is above the average in the neighbouring country. The Booth farm is nearer the average of the adjacent lands which it would be intended to serve.

The minister remarked
that a man going in for agriculture should not count the cost; he should just work away without giving any consideration to that question. The minister touches a very vital point when he makes this statement. If you look at the manufacturing industry you find that one of the first things they do is to count the cost. They take into consideration capital
Supply-Agriculture

expenditure and all expenses in connection with operation, and then they go to the utilities commission or some other commission and, getting their cost recognized at the figure they quote, they fix a profit of eight or ten per cent over and above that, and then a tariff on top of all that lest the industry fail. Now if a man is going into the business of agriculture why should not his calculations be made upon exactly the same basis? We have been talking about agricultural fairs. Perhaps I might mention that in the town of Olds, Alberta, in the constituency from which my hon. friend (Mr. Speakman) comes, they have induced a number of students to attend the agricultural college; and so keen is the interest which these young men are taking in their studies that it has been found necessary to increase the dormitory accommodation this year from one hundred to two hundred and fifty students. These young men are filled with delight at the prospect of taking up agriculture. They are taught everything that relates to the industry and are acquiring a love for the country. In my judgment there could be nothing more tragic than to have these prospective farmers, on leaving college with a roseate picture of farm life, disillusioned when they have to face the actual facts of farming as it is carried on in the country. The finer things in connection with farming have been expatiated upon to-day, but it would be a sad thing to see these young men, after taking up farms, drift away into the cities bankrupt because of their inability to meet expenses. The department should take these facts into account and have agriculture placed on the same basis as industry.

It is all too true
that practical farmers are contemptuous of scientific methods, but a great many farmers are coming to the conclusion that this is an unsound policy. It is not wise, and they are coming to realize the benefits of experiment and of the application of scientific principles to the carrying on of their business. But when the practical farmers of Ontario read that the department is contemplating paying $600 an acre for an extension to the experimental farm in Ottawa they will naturally want to know whether the department also contemplates an experiment to prove that anyone can make a living paying such prices for land. At once they will say that there is something wrong with the purchase: either the minister and his advisers do not know the value of land, or the man from whom they bought it is a tool of the government, or something else equally nasty. If experi-

ments can be carried on in other parts of Canada as well as in Ottawa, surely it would be wiser to buy land which is not so close to the city; for $600 an acre is not the value of farm land. Such a purchase only lays scientific agricultural experiments open to the contempt of the practical farmer, and this is the feeling that generally prevails. As the hon. member (Mr. Adshead) says, boys who are attending agricultural schools are taught scientific methods, and they will have to apply those methods under practical conditions. The minister said something true when he suggested that there was no need to count the cost. The farmers have to work almost from the time they are born until they die, and if they are lucky they will be buried.

I can assure my
hon. friend that the owner of the Booth farm is not in league with the government.

I did not say so; I
said you might lay yourself open to the charge.

That is one of the alternatives; either we do not know the price of land or we are in league with someone. I have had two or three conversations with this gentleman and I do not blame him for trying to get all he can out of the government. That is a common practice. On the other hand, it is my business to protect the treasury, and' that is one reason why I say I should not be the one to determine the question on behalf of the government. The exchequer court is the proper authority. I do not want to go to my hon. friend's constituency afterwards and have it said that it was I who paid $600. The fair way to settle the matter is to let the exchequer court, with all the evidence before it in regard to the value of adjoining lands, adjudicate and decide the amount.

The responsibility for
the selection of the site would be yours.

As regards the
comment I made respecting the cost of clearing land, I wonder how many gentlemen in this house who have cleaned heavy timber land would have jumped joyfully into the work if they had calmly contemplated the cost. I do not want to terrify anybody, and while I am aware of the biblical injunction to sit down and figure out the cost, I think that applies rather to building a house than to clearing land. I take off my hat to the old pioneer settlers of Canada, those of the maritime provinces and of Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia, who had to establish

Supply-Agriculture
farms in heavily wooded' lands. I do not fancy that they sat down and calculated the cost, because they had no cash to start with. They built up their farms by their strong right arm, working hard from early mom till dewy eve.

They did not pay $600
an acre.

Nor were there any high-powered tractors or donkey engines to take out the stumps in those days; they had to do it themselves. Many farms I know of were originally cleared by means of a two-year old steer at the short end of the yoke and a fourteen-year old boy at the other.

Would the minister like
a boy of his to be at one end of the yoke?

Yes. if necessary,
and I should be proud to think that he was capable of it.
Oh, oh!

There is no "oh,
oh!" about it. What would they have done in the old days when they were on part ration from the British government and had to use every device they could think of in order to be self-sustaining? If one boy would not do I would put two on. I am talking about conditions one hundred years ago; I am not advocating this method to-day.

The hon. member for
East Calgary has asked a question about counting the cost. I would ask him, as a pioneer I understand in western Canada, just how many would have pioneered in that country if they had counted the cost. Those of us who pioneered did not count the cost in dollars and cents, and some of us are probably living to-day to see the harvest reaped from those early efforts of ours.
Now that this estimate is up I feel I should be remiss in my duty if I were not to mention that in my constituency we have an experimental farm. It was established some years ago. I was one of the early pioneers in that country, and I am sure that the assistance it has given to the farmers in that section of the country cannot be measured in dollars and cents. When the great western plains were opened, particularly that part known as the Tramping lake country, extending between the northern and southern Saskatchewan rivers, the territory was wholly new and we had to experiment. It has been repeatedly said during this discussion that the farmer cannot afford to experiment, but I must say that we were greatly pleased when the Scott experimental farm was
established, demonstrating to us not only the kinds of grains we should grow, but also the varieties of fruits and trees that were best suited to that area. On the first of July, as is our custom, we had a field day at the Scott experimental farm, and I am not exaggerating when I say that there were seven thousand people gathered there. Almost any day in the summer, and particularly on Sundays, if you visit that farm you will find people there from as far south as Kindersley and Rosetown, as well as from a great distance to the west and north. I hope that this estimate will be approved by the committee.
I have a great deal of sympathy with the hon. member for Skeena because the country in which I pioneered twenty-two years ago was then in the same condition as the area for which he is pleading to-day. I think it behooves this or any other government in Canada to establish experimental farms or stations as circumstances warrant in any large section such as the Skeena country, and the government should be encouraged to do so.

I have been very much
interested in the recital of the early experiences of the Minister of Agriculture in Saskatchewan. With a two-year old steer at one end of the plough and the Minister of Agriculture at the other, I should have thought it would have been a very pertinent question to ask, which is the bull?
I have been rather impressed with what has been said concerning the central experimental farm and the purchase of high priced lands. In considering the situation we must be careful to remember that the overhead expense is on the central farm already, and if you buy land for one hundred or two hundred dollars an acre situated at some distance from headquarters, it is eventually going to cost you just as much as to buy land near the farm for five or six hundred dollars an acre, when you take into account new buildings and the great loss of time through running back and forth between the central farm and the new purchase.
Another point that I would stress is that an experimental farm can never be in the ordinary commercial sense a profitable farm. The profit from an experimental farm is lying in the files and records of experiments which have been completed by these farms, and in the information which has been printed and distributed Tor the use of farmers throughout the country. Everyone must realize that when you are farming on a plot of one-fortieth of an acre, with the large
Supply-Agriculture

amount of handwork and labour necessary under those conditions, you can never hope to make that farm a commercial success.
The statement has been made that the cost of clearing land in British Columbia would be $500 an acre if you wanted to establish an experimental farm there. I cannot allow that statement to go unchallenged. I pointed out a little earlier in the afternoon that British Columbia is an immense country, with varying conditions. In some places the timber is very heavy; in other places it would hardly be necessary to do any clearing at all. It is true there is not much land of the latter kind, but in the dry belt there are many areas that can be ploughed with comparatively little work, and that would be principally the removal of stone and brush. However, with regard to the big problems in connection with land clearing in British Columbia, we feel that one of the most important is that of making use of the waste material which remains on the ground after our high lead system of logging has removed the commercial timber from the land. That is a problem which I think the research council should investigate very carefully to see if we cannot get some revenue from the use of these waste products through the development of salable by-products of various kinds. Scientists have informed me that there are excellent chances for development along these lines. In clearing land in British Columbia in the ordinary farming sense-at all events if there is a Scotchman at the helm-the land first cleared is that which is most easily cleared. You get the slash off your land and sell the timber for what you can get; then after you have done the burning you at once seed the land down, and you find that grass easily takes hold with the little dressing of potash that there is in the ashes left on the surface. Then you graze it with sheep or goats, which will eat off the grass and the young willow sprouts so that the willows will not grow up again; and when the stumps begin to rot, you commence your land clearing as opportunity offers. You can begin to take your stumps out at the end of eighteen months or two years, using either powder or stumping machines, whichever is the cheaper. There is a great variety of land out there, and some of it will cost from forty to fifty dollars an acre to clear, under the conditions I have described.

I am afraid that
unless I make a further remark about pioneering a wrong impression may be left in the minds of those who are listening to this discussion or who read the report. In order to 
counteract the shock which the hon. member for Bow River got at the thought of human labour being used in the way I have described, and to satisfy the curiosity of the hon. member (Mr. Tolmie) as to who was the fourteen-year old boy, let me say that I was speaking of conditions in Ontario one hundred years ago, and I do not think you will figure that I was very much in evidence at that time. So far as counting the cost is concerned, whether it be in labour and privation either in the east or on the prairie, there is no one that I know of who has the real farming or home-building instinct who does not feel that all the labour and hardships were worth while once he experiences the joy of owning his own land and of having his own roof over his head.

May I suggest that
though the minister may not be one hundred years old he may be one hundred years behind the times.
That is the contribution of the hon. member for New Westminster.

Apparently this
is a field day for the farmers; and as we have heard from every other province in the Dominion I think I might say a word in regard to Prince Edward Island. I wish to speak in favour of these experimental plots. In my county I think we have three of them, and they have proved very successful and very beneficial. I wish to refer for a moment to the experimental farm or station in connection with the fox industry at Summerside. I think the minister has just said that that experimental station cost around $14,000 a year. To my mind there is no better expenditure of public money in the Dominion than that incurred in connection with that experimental station. Last year it was estimated that the silver fox trade from Prince Edward Island alone, including live foxes and furs, amounted to something over $3,000,000, and when you apply that to the whole Dominion you have some idea of what the silver fox business means to this country. It is regrettable that the people of Canada are not engaging in that industry to a greater extent than they are. The people of the European countries are going in for it very strongly. This year we had hundreds of buyers from European countries, especially from Norway, who bought large quantities of the best of our breeding stock and took them over to Europe. The experimental station at Summerside is doing excellent work. The breeders contributed a large number of the foxes to that station; the

government did not have to buy them, and the work is being carried on by Doctor Ennis Smith, formerly of Ottawa. The information published in the bulletin Doctor Smith is getting out will be of great benefit to breeders.
I wish to ask the minister a question in connection with the work at the central experimental farm in the matter of clover which will withstand the winter climate of eastern Canada. One of the greatest difficulties the farmers in Prince Edward Island meet is to get a clover which will carry through the winter and from which they can expect to get a second crop. At this farm in Ottawa a few years ago I was shown a plot which I was informed had been in clover for seven years, and it was still producing a splendid crop. I should like to know if any advances have been made in that direction and if the minister has any information which he can give us along that line. It is an important question to our people; if we can get a clover which will give us two or three crops it will be a great advantage and a great help to us. At present we sow clover seed very extensively; we get a crop one year, but in another year it is gone.

Well, there is an
increase in the work all along the line in the various laboratories and a very considerable increase is due to the flat rate increase to the staff of $120. That takes quite a bit of it. Then take the root rot question in the west, the new insect pests and new enemies all along the line, which increase the necessity of preparing to fight them.

Does that necessitate the
employment of some new men?

It will necessitate
engaging some new men.
How many?

We have just decided to establish a new staff, one man being already engaged, and we have already secured one of them at the university at Edmonton. The Hon. Mr. Hoadley of Alberta has drawn my attention to the fact-and I have been aware of it myself for about eight years- that one of the species of root rot is making considerable headway in northern Saskatchewan and Alberta. We have done a good good deal of work, but it is now developing into a very potent enemy. It lives in the soil and there is no way of killing it except by sterilizing the soil, which would be impossible without a laboratory equipment. That has been supplied by the Alberta university, and we are going to provide the men. We hope to carry out a working arrangement with Alberta similar to that which we entered into with the Manitoba government with respect to the rust laboratory in Winnipeg. We put up the building, and the provincial government supplied the land, power, heat and water.
What plants are attacked by the root rot?

Cereals and a certain number of our native grasses. It is not known whether the disease was imported from

speechtext:
There is no information, I take it,
that my hon. friend requires in regard to this vote. The amount is practically the same as last year-there is a light increase.

The hon. member says
that the first two items in the vote are interdepartmental accounts. Is that so?
They are very largely departmental.

I would remind the minister that I pointed out to him last year that in the estimates for 1926 there was a vote of $10,000 for a post office at Mahone Bay. That item was not included in the estimates for last year, and the minister gave me many ingenious and conflicting reasons why it was not included. I wonder if he could tell me why it has not been found necessary to revote that money this year.

I am afraid I cannot add
anything to what I said to my genial friend last year. The condition of things is much the same as it was a year ago.

Apparently it is going to
stay that way.
Why is the tractor required for postal purposes at Truro not charged to the Post Office department?

That department makes
the request to the Department of Public Works for a tractor to carry the mail back and forth, and we supply it.

Why should it not be
charged to the Post Office department?

Apparently everybody
comes to the Department of Public Works.

I should like to ask the
minister definitely if the administration has concluded that the expenditure at Mahone Bay will not be made. Has the administration definitely abandoned the idea of erecting a public building there?

Perhaps I should say to
my hon. friend that Mahone Bay is in the same situation as a number of other places as to which similarly urgent requests have been made none of which are included in these estimates. By that statement I do not mean to say that these works are definitely abandoned. They will receive consideration just as soon as it is possible to get the money to carry out the work.

Will the minister not tell
me why that work is not necessary now if it was necessary in 1926? Business has expanded since then and the Minister of Finance has spoken about a handsome surplus this year. If in the state of public finances in 1926 the work in question was necessary, why is it not necessary this year?

Apparently there are more urgent needs now to provide for the increased business of the country than there were in 1926. That is the best explanation I can give my hon. friend. In the opinion of the departmental officials, from the reports we get other works are really more urgently required in order to facilitate the carrying on of the business of the country. I think that is all I can say.

Is that a reasonable excuse to give the committee in face of the fact that there is an increase of $15,000 over the previous year for repairs to the royal Canadian naval barracks and wharves in the dockyard at Halifax, although we have no navy?

There is a principle involved in this matter. An appropriation wras made in 1926 for a building at Mahone Bay. Obviously that money would not have been placed in the estimates had it not been required for the public service. I know that with respect to certain western appropriations the war necessitated their being withdrawn and dropped, and a change of government has prevented their ever finding a place in the appropriations since. But here you have a public building that in the opinion of the then government-and the same government is in office to-day-was a necessity. The item for that public building is now dropped, and I think this house has a right to know exactly why it is dropped. If it is for political reasons, say so and be done with it. If it wras in order that when the election came on you might have all your votes for public buildings that year for the purpose of influencing public opinion, as has been done in the past, let it be admitted. Let there be frankness in this matter; let us know exactly why this appropriation has been dropped. I think it is not an unfair thing for the committee to know the reason.

I am perfectly willing to answer any question asked by my hon. friend, or by any other hon. member opposite. I would call my hon. friend's attention, to this very vote, No. 123, and ask him to tell the committee whether he really thinks these particular estimates for Nova Scotia were prepared with a view to meeting political exigencies, when the fact is that there is in the estimates not a vote in favour of that province so far as any of the ridings represented by members on the government side are concerned. I do not object to that; it is quite within the rights of my hon. friends to refer to it. I direct the attention
of the minister to the fact that the appropriation in question was apparently required in the public interests in 1926. A gentleman named Duff was defeated in that constituency in the election of that year, and he has stated that upon his having so requested the item was dropped from the estimates. That is the reason he gave last year for its having been abandoned. Now, is the public service of this country to be thus conducted? That is the question that this house has a right to have satisfactorily answered. Is the hon. gentleman who now represents Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff), and who stated in this house that he advised that the vote be withdrawn from the estimates, to determine whether the community affected shall or shall not be given a public building? The country has a right to know, and I submit that the minister should give the committee an explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is making a slight mistake when he says that this vote was included in the estimates by the government now in office. He will remember that between the government of that day and the present administration there was another government which held office for three months.

speechtext:
I would point out that
the Minister of Public Works at that time was not the present minister, and the two might have had different ideas regarding the necessity for a public building there.

We are entitled to
something better than that.
