Will the minister oxplain the item, "Truro-tractor for postal purposes, 31,300."?

This vote is to provide

I am glad to learn from
the minister that the postal business of Truro is growing so rapidly as to necessitate the use of a tractor for the moving of mails. This brings up the question of the post office building at that point, which was erected some forty-four or forty-five years ago. At that time the population of the town was about three thousand; to-day it is approximately three times three thousand. Every effort has been made in recent years to provide a suitable building for the requirements of the people in Truro, and about 1912 or 1913 the department sent down an architect named Mr. Rankin to look over the situation. After several days spent there he worked out a plan which he presented to the government with an estimate of the cost of remodelling the building, but after considering the question the government decided that it would not pay to remodel it. It was felt that the cost would be too high and that even with the proposed remodelling the town would still have an old building. The building to-day is in very bad condition, and the cost being paid upon the repairs year after year would almost cover the interest charges on a new structure. I regret to tell the house that the site which was purchased for the new building in that town in 1914 for $17,000 had been sold at a loss to the country of nearly $10,000-$9,200 to be exact. As happened in other places during recent years there was a considerable decline in real estate values there, but nothing to warrant the lot being sold at such a loss. It seems to me that,

in view of the many promises which the town has received for the construction of a new post office building, it is not very creditable to the government that this ideal lot-in fact, the most suitable lot-should have been sold at such a loss. I regret exceedingly that there is no mention whatever in these estimates of any proposal for a new building in the town of Truro. The minister may depend upon it that the day is not very far distant when a new post office building will have to be erected there. Is the $7,500 for the

It is an addition.

Returning to Mahone
Bay, I think a frank explanation should be given the committee; ministerial sidestepping of the question is not altogether the thing for us. The Minister of Public Works has the advantage now of having his deputy beside him. Will he tell us on whose advice the estimate of 1926 was prepared? What officer of the department recommended the construction of the building, and what officer of the department recommended the withdrawal of the item? It is within the recollection of a good many in this house that during last session the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough informed the committee that the vote had been struck out on his advice. And he happened to be the defeated candidate for the constituency of Queens-Lunenburg. Why was the building not necessary after his defeat if it was necessary before the election? That estimate was passed in the spring of 1926, when the government of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was in power. True, the personnel of the government has changed in the interval, but the government in power to-day is to all intents and purposes the same. If in the judgment of the government of that day it was necessary to construct the building in 1926, what has taken place in the interval to cause the government to change its view? And if it did change its view, as obviously it has done, on whose advice did it do so? The committee is entitled to know.

Of course there have been a great many changes since 1926. In regard to this item I should be very glad to obtain for my hon. friend any information which is in the departmental files. The information we have here relates only to the items that
are in the estimates. My hon, friend will readily understand in view of the large number of post offices and harbours throughout the country that one cannot bear in mind all the things relating to these post offices and harbours that are not mentioned in the estimates. I remember the discussion last year. All I can say to my hon. friend is that the situation is no different now from what it was when this house last year decided that the reasons then given were perhaps the best that could be given as to why an item was not included at that time. I should think that the point of my hon. friend's suggestion-it is more than a suggestion; it is almost a statement-that this has been omitted for political reasons is completely answered when you see that there is no provision made in the estimates for any post offices in the province of Nova Scotia in any ridings represented by Liberals.
There were in 1926 prior to the election.
I was mot in the department at that time.
That does not answer the question at all. Why not ask the deputy?

If the minister was at all familiar with the situation in Mahone Bay in 1926 he would have realized that a vote was included in the estimates that year because there was a pressing need in the community. The present building is entirely inadequate. It is small, cramped, in fact it is unsightly, and it is in one of the prettiest little country towns in Nova Scotia. The reasons which made this expenditure necessary in 1926 are even more cogent to-day. I should like to know from the minister if the statement made by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough last year was correct, that he had that item withdrawn from the estimates. If he is unable to answer, I suggest that the items stand until he gets the information.
I do not think I had an interview with the hon. member for An-tigonish-Guysborough while these estimates were being prepared.
I was referring to last year's estimates.

That is a year further
away, and perhaps my recollection does not serve me quite so well. What my hon. friend says about the building being worse now than it was two years ago does not apply only to the post office at Mahone Bay. The same
Supply-Public Works

is true of a number of post offices from one end of this country to the other; it is true with regard to a number of post offices down in Nova Scotia, places at which post offices are not being provided for in these estimates.

I think the minister should answer the question. I do not know whether he is in a position to contradict or affirm the statement made by the hon. member for Antigonfish-Guysborough. I suggest that the item stand until some better explanation can be given.
May I call attention to the fact, Mr. Chairman, that we are not now voting on an item for Mahone Bay? That is not before the committee.
We are voting on the estimates for public buildngs for the province of Nova Scotia, and I am suggesting that such an item should be there.

I personally would like very much to hear the minister answer that question. Of course I have often heard such charges as are being made here to-night, and have put them down as political talk, but I should like to know what are the facts in regard to this matter. Is it true what the hon. member says? I think the minister might well give an answer.

The minister has said
that by looking at the estimates one would at once realize that political considerations did not influence the government in the preparation of the estimates for Nova Scotia. Knowing what we do with respect to certain public expenditures contemplated in Halifax, we have not the least doubt that the minister for that province is responsible for these estimates, and we do know that nothing is in the estimates at this time for Nova Scotia, but at the appropriate moment there may be sums available in order to secure the votes of the electorate of that province when election time comes round. There is no question about that at all. We have it in relation to what took place in Halifax not long since, and I say that it is high time that the provinces should not be deprived of their due portion of public moneys for public services required in order that those sums may be put in the estimates at the fitting moment for the purpose of influencing public opinion at the time of an election.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Surely my
hon. friend does not suggest, and surely no hon. member from Nova Scotia would enter-
tain the belief, that any expenditures made by the government in the great port and city of Halifax would be made for political purposes? Surely not.

Surely not? I happen
to know the hon. gentleman's history in that regard in his own province, and it is so nearly alike to what I suggested a moment ago that there is no doubt at all that at the appropriate time the discussion with respect to expenditures in Halifax, which are not these expenditures at all, will come before the house, and I say that the same directing mind that desired to prevent and that did prevent, expenditures there is responsible for there being no provision for public expenditure in Nova Scotia in the estimates at this time. I say it is not fitting that the province should thus be deprived of public moneys necessary for carrying on the public services.
There is an item occupying a full page of estimates for Nova Scotia.

That is under harbours and rivers; I am not discussing those particular expenditures. It is the " harbours and rivers" touch this year, you see; it may be dredging next. My hon. friend seems to understand the allusion. The point I desire to make is this: Having regard to what did transpire, and to this expenditure for harbours and rivers, about which there is a singular history in Nova Scotia-is the Minister of the Interior familiar with that history?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have voted a lot of estimates for Nova Scotia.
For harbours and rivers?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Yes, and
dry docks.

I think the item should stand because this is the only occasion upon which an opportunity will arise for the discussion of the question of public buildings in Nova Scotia. That question is limited to this one item, No. 123; that is all the public buildings there are for Nova Scotia. With respect to New Brunswick the policy seems to be very clear, that dredging, not being very spectacular, will be done this year, but when you come to Quebec and Ontario and the other provinces you will find quite a number of items for public buildings. For instance, I see an item of $15,000 to finish a public building at Wainwright. The Minister of the Interior might be able to explain that.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I am quite ready.
Supply-Public Works

Saskatchewan stands in
much the same position. Certain buildings there have been started and have to be
finished. It is the same with respect to Manitoba. In Quebec there are a considerable number, in Montreal alone quite a number of items, involving large sums of money. The minister realizes that that is so, but the item we are discussing is the only one with respect to public buildings in Nova Scotia, and I certainly desire to know what has been done by the province of Nova Scotia that it should be penalized because in the exercise of a sound discretion it did not see fit to yield to the views that were pressed upon it by the Minister of National Defence. Surely you cannot penalize a province for not taking bad advice, if the Minister of Justice suggests that that is what should be done. I say no; they should be rewarded.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would not penalize
them, I think they suffer enough by the representation they have.

It is a singular thing
that that is exactly what the electors of Halifax thought when they rejected the Minister of National Defence. I do think the minister must be fair with this committee and tell us what were the guiding principles which led to Mahone Bay, with all its requirements, being denied the post office which the Prime Minister said the government accepted the responsibility for. The utterances of the hon. member, whose classic smile we are all delighted to see in this house, whether he is edifying us with an account of the wrongs of the auditor general or the advantages of doing dredging work at the proper season in Nova Scotia-these are a matter of profound indifference. But I do submit that the minister should give us some explanation.

I am sure we are all pleased
to see that the hon. member is taking an interest in an item of $10,000 which was dropped from the estimates last year in regard to public works in Nova Scotia. He seems to think there was some political influence brought to bear when this item was dropped. That is quite true, and perhaps if I give the house the reason why it was dropped the leader of the opposition will be satisfied. I might say that when I asked the previous Minister of Public Works to include in the estimates an amount for the building at Mahone Bay politics was furthest from my thoughts.
Carried.

Hon. members are saying
"carried" because they do not want to hear 56103-38
the explanation. But after I had worked two years with the Minister of Public Works to get the item in the estimates and the announcement was made to the world that such an amount had been' provided for, the very gentlemen who said I was playing politics were the father and the brother of the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg. Consequently when I found that politics were being played I advised the minister-I do not know whether or not he took my advice-to drop the item; because, Mr. Chairman, as I said a moment ago, I did not have politics in my mind when I asked for it. I did not want politics to interfere, and when my hon. friend said I was playing politics and the post office would never be built, I thought it my duty to tell the Minister of Public Works, the architect and everybody else that the building at the present time was not necessary.

It seems to me this would be
an opportune time for us to take counsel together in regard to the expenditure of public money in Nova Scotia or in any other province where the amount is only $10,000 for a public building. I know nothing about the amount that was dropped from the estimates, but if only $10,000 is required, if that is all that locality needs, it would be well for us her'e and now to scrutinize all such amounts for public buildings in Canada. There is hardly any way of ascertaining what may have been in the mind of the hon. member or of the government, but we ought to recognize that the appropriating of public money for the purpose of getting votes is a delusion. My hon. friends across the way laugh, because they have been guilty, as perhaps another party may have been guilty, of voting public money for public buildings where their candidates were more often defeated than elected, and I think rightly so. Public money ought to be wisely voted and wisely expended. We all recognize that in our own municipalities we desire public money to be spent and large buildings erected, thus creating a vast liability upon the country and the government. We have throughout Ontario- and I assume it is true in other provinces- buildings going to decay, buildings which are of no commercial use, of no commercial value, which ought to be sold to insurance companies. If they cannot be sold to those companies then they should be sold by public tender and auction, in order to reduce the overhead as far as the government is concerned. We have an opportunity of recognizing, I think, that the expenditure of public money is a matter that should be judiciously and carefully scrutinized, and we should also recognize that the expenditure of public

Supply-Public Works

money where it is not necessary is not a vote-getter, but rather recoils against the parties who do that for the purpose of electing a candidate or promoting their interests in an election. Before spending money we should look into it as a business proposition, and knowing what has happened in these small communities we ought to rise to the occasion and spend public money only where it is requisite and necessary.

Will the minister tell
me what is intended to be done in regard to the building at New Glasgow which I spoke to him about? Is it the intention of the government to provide in the supplementary estimates of this year for the necessary alterations to that building?

I recollect the New
Glasgow matter on account of the interviews I had with my hon. friend in regard to it, but there is no decision to make public expenditures this year other than those we are asking for in the estimates that are now before the house. I know of no decision in regard to any buildings other than those asked for here.

May I remind the hon. minister that I had what I consider to be a distinct undertaking on his part that he would this year, in the preparation of his estimates, include an amount for that building and recommend it to council? Am I not correct in that?

I would not like to say
to my hon. friend or to anybody else that anybody has had anything amounting to a definite undertaking from me since I have been in charge of this department to provide any building at any place. I remember the interview I had with my hon. friend. I recall very well the strong^ilea put forward, but I have no recollection of making any definite promise to him or to anyone else that what he asked for would be done.

I think I can refresh
the minister's memory when I point out that in his office after we had discussed this matter he stated that he would make a memorandum in regard to it, so that he would have next year a clear understanding and recollection of what we had discussed and what we had arrived at. I think if he will look in his office he will find that memorandum, and the statement I have made will, I am sure, be borne out by that memorandum. I ask him again to include in the supplementary estimates this year an amount sufficient to carry out the suggested alteration in that building. He is thoroughly

aware, and so is his deputy, of the necessities of the case. The matter has been presented to him not only by myself but also by the Liberal candidate in the county and others who are thoroughly aware of the situation. It is not fair to treat the people of New Glasgow as he has been treating them during the last two years, and I appeal to him to do justice. I recollect very distinctly the interviews we had.

Mr. Chairman, while I do not claim to remember all the details of the situation, I recall very distinctly the interviews to which my hon. friend refers. I would remind him that the representations made to me with respect to the condition of the building at New Glasgow are not by any means more urgent or-shall I say?-pathetic than those which have been made on behalf of at least fifty other places throughout the country. There is a strong demand for public buildings to provide for post offices, customs and other public services. My hon. friend must recollect that I do not get anything like the money for this department that I ask the treasury board and the Minister of Finance for, but I can assure him that I shall be very glad to look up the memorandum and reconsider the requirements of New Glasgow along with those of other towns when these matters are receiving attention.

We discussed this case last session, and at that time I thought the minister had committed himself; I think so still. There is not very much use in telling the committee that other towns are asking for public buildings; I am not interested in them at all. The fact is, the situation in New Glasgow is intolerable. The minister knows it, his officials know it. Two different plans were made and submitted, and then revised plans were made. All the facts are thoroughly well known to the department and to the minister, and again I ask him to implement what I understood to be the definite promise given by him to me last session.

What my hon. friend regards as a promise, Mr. Chairman, shows how dangerous it would be for me now or at any other time to say positively that anything will be done to carry out his request. I do not think he will go so far as to say that I have definitely promised to look after his requirements in respect of New Glasgow. Nor do I think that any hon. members on either side of the house will say that in regard to any of the representations they have made to me-and they have been fairly importunate-I have ever given a definite assur-

ance in their favour until the votes asked for appeared in the estimates. As I have already said, I have to convince the treasury board and council of the necessity for these expenditures before they can be passed, and sometimes I have trouble even after getting my estimates beyond that stage.

I was much surprised at the admission of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) that he had prevailed on the minister in a moment-shall I say?-of weakness to agree to the item of $10,000 for Mahone Bay being dropped. Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. I made a certain statement about two persons who deliberately said I was playing politics in regard to this item, and I submit the hon. member is absolutely out of order in questioning my statement.

Explanation!

Mr. Chairman, last year I brought to the attention of the minister, and the year before to the attention of his predecessor, the deplorable and inadequate condition of the postal service in the town of Oxford, Nova Scotia. The Department of Public Works is fully aware, as is also the department of the Postmaster General, of the conditions existing there. The post office in Oxford is conducted in a shack. A plan has been submitted to the department showing the inadequate accommodation. Not only so, but resolutions have been passed by the town council and petitions have been presented by the ratepayers and the board of trade praying that some remedy be applied, and suitable premises be acquired. It seems to me that the post office service in all parts of Canada should be maintained at a certain standard at least. The standard of the postal service in Oxford is a disgrace to the Dominion. I brought this to the attention of the minister last session, and it is my purpose to do so every session until this condition of things is remedied. I would ask the Minister of Public Works to reconsider the statement he made to-night and include in the supplementary estimates a vote to provide at least decent postal accommodation for Oxford. I might point out that Oxford is a very important postal centre, a great many rural routes radiating from it. The people served by the post office at this important centre are entitled to better conditions. The population of the town is approximately 1,500, and the annual revenue of the post office is upwards of $5,000. If I mistake not, two or three years ago the Post Office Department, through some-of its officials, recommended that better accommodation be provided at this point.

I shall be very glad to
go into the matter carefully, but it is quite impossible for me to say at the moment what may be the outcome. We will give the hon. member's request the very best consideration that we are capable of.

While the minister
seems to be so lavish in dealing with Nova

Scotia, I should like to remind him that there is in my county a small town, St. Fabien, with a population of three thousand, which needs a post office very badly. I hope when he is considering the demands coming from hon. gentlemen opposite he will not forget the county of Rimouski.

sir, that by the time all these other requests Teceive consideration there will be no money left.

the New Glasgow post office yet. That building was constructed about fifty years ago, at a time when the population of the town and the immediately surrounding country which it serves was very much less than it is to-day. The situation there is very acute, as the minister knows.
Order.

Who is talking about
order now? Last year plans were submitted to the minister; later, after discussion with his staff, revised plans were prepared and submitted to him; we discussed the whole situation on several separate occasions, and in the end I received, from the minister, as I said before, what I considered to be a definite gentleman's agreement that he would put in the estimates for the present year, and submit to and support before the treasury board, an amount sufficient for this work. Shall we be able to make
certain observations with regard to public buildings when the Quebec vote is reached?
