speechtext: Certainly.

Just on the point of order, Mr. Chairman; I have no wish to oppose the ruling, but I would like to get it quite clearly in my mind that under this

heading of public buildings it is only permissible to discuss those buildings already in Nova Scotia, or those which should be there.
Oh, oh.

I mean that literally. The discussion must not go beyond those buildings already there and other buildings which, in the opinion of members from that province, should be erected there. Is that right? A discussion of buildings in Ontario, for instance, would not be allowed at this time, in your judgment?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is right.

This discussion has been going on for some time, and without wanting to be unfair it does look as if Nova Scotia is being penalized. We have no vote at all for any public buildings in Nova Scotia while there are ten votes for Quebec immediately following, totalling over a million dollars. I would like to know why that condition has come about. Last year a delegation from my county came to Ottawa asking for the construction of a post office in the town of New Waterford. This is an incorporated town with a population of over 10,000 and the post office is in the back part of an old store. That delegation was composed of prominent Liberals from that county, and I refrained from accompanying them or from taking any part in the matter for fear the government might believe I was after some credit. I thought there would be a vote last year; I understood the delegation received assurances that something would be done for them, and I know they are looking for a vote this year. Surely such principles are not going to be tolerated, the government is not going to sit by quietly and allow such implications to be made, as we heard from the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff). However, that building was either needed in Mahone Bay or it was not needed. If it was not needed the amount should not have been placed in the estimates, but once there it should not have been removed to suit the political desires of my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough, for whom I have the utmost respect.
I want to plead again with the Minister of Public Works, and to ask him if he will not consider the necessity of the town of New Waterford. I venture to say that of all the applications now before the government or to come before the government, none are

Supply-Public IForfcs
more1 deserving than, that of the town of New Waterford. I submit the matter to the Minister of Public Works in the hope that he will consider it when making up the supplementary estimates.

I know something about the town referred to by my hon. friend, and the post office there is doing a good business; if I am correctly informed there is quite a mining business there. It is just like many other places; it would be much better if a new public building could be erected, but as I recollect from our reports I do not think the condition of the building can compare with that of some of the others which we have had to refuse. However, I shall be very glad to give the question consideration when the supplementary estimates are made up. By doing that I do not want to be understood as making a promise that this will appear in the supplementary estimates, because I am not going to do that with regard to any application.

I am sorry my hon. friend thought it necessary to criticize any remarks I made, especially in view of the fact that I am very strongly in sympathy with the idea of a new post office building in New Waterford. Last year, when this delegation was here, although it was entirely outside any constituency in which I have any interest, either as the member or otherwise, I accompanied these gentlemen; I do not see why the hon. member did not come along, but I was good enough to take this delegation to see certain influential persons in Ottawa, and the least he might do is to give me credit without criticizing me. Again within the last month I had a very strong telegram from a prominent citizen of New Waterford asking me to get a vote put in the estimates for a new post office for that town, and again I approached influential members of parliament in regard to the matter, so I think the least my hon. friend might do is to thank me for my good intentions.

Far be it from me to take away any credit at all from my hon. friend. I know exactly what he did last year and how enthusiastically he' worked, and if I have any regret at all it is that the influence of the hon. gentleman in having items included in the estimates is not so great as it is in having them removed therefrom.

I do not think it is fair
to the minister to ask all these picayune questions and make these trifling interjections at this time. We all realize they are inspired
more by politics than anything else. It is time we devoted our attention to business rather than to a controversy between two hon. members. It would seem from the arguments advanced here that when the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) was getting a public building it was politics in the eyes of my hon. friend opposite, but if the hon. member for Queens-Lunen-burg could get a public building it was good business. No one need be under the impression that only hon. members opposite have need of post offices. I think every member on this side has grievances in that regard which he could ventilate if he saw fit to do so. So much has been said about Mahone Bay that the time wasted and the expense-incurred through that discussion would represent a sum more than sufficient to build the whole town.
Very well, let us start.

Let the minister go on
with the public business, and if hon. members opposite have that interest in the public welfare which they claim to have they will show some desire to cooperate in the despatch of public business.

I was not aware that any
personal reflection had been cast by me upon the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough, although the hon. member who has just spoken suggested that there was. If there is any suggestion that I made any such reflection I deny it emphatically.
I want to ask the minister, in view of the explanation given by the hon. member (Mr. Duff)-I am doing it in all seriousness-for the dropping of this vote, if he will not give an assurance that this item will be placed in the supplementary estimates. I also think it is the duty of the minister to inform the committee as to whether the dictates of a member who may happen to be annoyed governs the policy of his department.
I never get annoyed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No, Mr. Chairman, I have
asked th.e minister two questions and I want to get answers to them.

I was astonished to find
that any member of this house thought the minister ever gave an assurance in a matter of this kind. I have been as importunate in the matter of post offices as any hon. member. There are post offices needed urgently in three different towns in my constituency, and I have not been able to get any assurance that they will be provided. Lest the minister
Supply-Public Works

may perhaps be impressed by requests from hon. gentlemen opposite I want to remind him, if there are to be any appropriations for post offices in the supplementary estimates, that I have three very urgent demands from my constituency.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Name.	.

You will have another
session.

I think the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) has put a question to the minister which affects every member of this house and every part of this Dominion. We have an hon. gentleman getting up in this house and declaring that at one time in his somewhat zig-zag political career he had importuned the government to build a post office in a certain place. Through the exigencies of politics he was obliged to run in. another constituency. Whether that fact had anything to do with bringing about a change in his mind or in his attitude we, of course, can only conjecture.
What do you think yourself?

We have it from the hon. gentleman's own statement that at one time he thought a post office should have been built in this place, and he importuned the government along that line. Now he goes to the government and asks them not to build a post office where formerly he said it was needed. The hon. member for Lunenburg has put a proper question to the minister in asking whether or not he subscribes to that doctrine. The minister, remains silent on the matter, and unless he answers the question I say that he is indicted as agreeing to that kind of policy and saying that he, in the expenditure of public money, is influenced by that spirit. It does not come well from the hon. member for Antigonish-Guys-borough, it seems to me, to say that there is no politics in this sort of thing. There is politics in it. Politics of the most partisan character is spread all over it.
Hear, hear.
I say it is up to the minister to answer that question. It was a proper question, and it should be answered in the public interests.
Carried.
Oh no, it is not carried.

I want to answer the question of my hon. friend if no other member has any questions to put before I do so. My hon. friend who has just spoken has

very properly urged the claims of a certain section of his riding to a public building, and I suppose there is no hon. gentleman here whose claims should be entitled to more consideration at my hands. He urged the matter sincerely upon my consideration, and I think he will agree with me that when I was not able to meet his views I was guided by official reports and the needs of various communities. That is what has actuated me in preparing these estimates. I do not want to cast any reflection on the criticisms which have been made, but those criticisms might have had some justification if either last year or this year any substantial number of post offices had been granted to constituencies represented by Liberals, Conservatives, Progressives or the members of any other political party. The grants for this purpose, since I have been in charge of the department, have been reduced to the barest minimum consistent with the necessities of public business. Now what we are considering is not a vote for Mahone Bay, or any other place in the riding represented by my genial friend; we are considering vote No. 123 involving an expenditure of $84,500, and the only objection that I have heard so far to that vote is that it is not large enouigh. There has not been one single objection against any item in that vote, and I do not consider the criticisms which have been made are well founded, in view of the fact that throughout the Dominion constituencies represented by both political parties have been treated in the matter of these grants in the same way.

We have heard a great deal about public buildings that are not included in the vote. I think perhaps it would be well for the committee to get down to business and discuss the items that are actually before us.

The question has not yet
been answered; in fact, two or three questions have been asked the minister and so far he has failed to reply. It is idle for the minister to get up before an intelligent committee like this and discuss other post offices which may be in the estimates but which are not in this particular vote. This is a specific instance wherein a post office was recommended by the officers of the Public Works department. Can we have that report? What were the reasons given by the officers of the department when the building was originally authorized? I assume it was stated in that report that the building was urgently required. Who, then, was the officer that made the report? Has any officer of the department either withdrawn or overridden that report, or does the report still stand1 as indicating the view of the department, and is it among the files of the department? And why was the item withdrawn? If it was urgently needed in 1926 why is it not needed tc-day? We were told yesterday that there is some $40,000,000 of a surplus in the treasury. Why not implement this promise made to the people of Mahone Bay prior to the election of 1926? Cannot the minister answer this question in a direct way instead of side-stepping, as he did five minutes ago when the question was put? Does he approve a procedure whereby a defeated candidate in a particular constituency can override the vote of the House of Commons and say, "Drop that item, I was beaten in that constituency"? If that is not playing politics in an important department of government, then I do not know what is. This committee demands some explanation of that procedure.

I thought my hon. friend
was in the house when I made the explanation-

I have been here all
evening.

-that so far as the decision was concerned as to what should be included in the estimates, I took the reports that were before me at the time the estimates were being prepared and arrived at the best conclusion I could. I have no recollection of my hon. friend having interviewed me; I know he did not interview me this year in connection with Mahone Bay or any other place.
Nor last year either.

I do not recall his having
interviewed me. My recollection is that for a considerable period of the session, while the estimates were under preparation he was not in the house. Naturally, my recollection of the matter is not as vivid as it was a year ago, but I know that for reasons that were considered sufficient then the vote was passed without an item for Mahone Bay. I want to assure my hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) that there is no ground for his standing up and saying, upon an examination of these estimates, that they have been prepared with a view to meeting political emergencies.
I have said so.
Well, I say it is not so.

We must all admire the
ingenuity of the minister; he has been asked half a dozen times to answer a simple question and he has skated around it about as smoothly as anyone I have seen in the house. This, I submit, ought to be done: until the minister is able to answer the questions that have been put by the hon. member for Frontenac and the hon. member for South Wellington the item should stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What is the question?

Upon what grounds was that post office recommended for Mahone Bay? We should have the report of the officials and then we should have an explanation as to why the item was withdrawn. That is what this side of the house is asking for, and that is what the minister will not give us. He has shown himself, I must admit, extremely clever in getting around the question, but I do not think we shall be satisfied until we have been given an explanation as to why this building was recommended, what was considered the necessity for it, why the item was withdrawn, and whether the minister gave his approval. Does the minister approve of the principle of a defeated candidate having an item removed from the estimates?

The minister is being attacked as a very astute politician. May I point out that the hon. member for South Wellington stepped in at an opportune moment while the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. MacNutt) was discussing some property that had been bought at one time

Supply-Public Works
by 'the department and had subsequently been sold at a very much lower figure-at a loss of $10,000, I think. If this item has to stand pending the obtaining of information for the committee, I should like to have the minister bring down information showing when this particular lot was bought, by whom, and from whom. The fact that such a lot as the one referred to in the locality mentioned by the hon. member for Colchester was bought at a sum representing $10,000 more than its present value is something that does not look very good, at least to me. The hon. gentleman says that the town has grown and its business is greater than it was before; but certain property purchased by the Conservative government is not worth nearly as much to-day as the money originally paid for it. I say, I want to find out whom the property was purchased from.

The hon.
member makes one statement which will apply generally to the whole Dominion. He says that in this particular case property purchased while the Conservative government was in power is not worth nearly so much to-day under a Liberal administration. I am not going to quarrel with the hon. gentleman on that point; probably he is right. The people of Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, are realizing that property is not worth as much to-day under this government as it was some years ago.
I say it is not worth what was paid for it.

The hon.
gentleman speaks of the opportuneness with which certain members get up on this side, but I notice that he did not give the Minister of Public Works a chance to rise and reply to the hon. member (Mr. Hocken). The hon. member for Moose Jaw put himself in the breach to protect the minister or to give him a little longer time to think the thing over. Well, I submit that in all conscience the minister has had sufficient time to think it over. He might avoid for the time being the tactics which he evidently learned from that venerable Liberal statesman, Oliver Mowat, who used always to say, whenever any embarrassing question was asked him, "I shall take it into my most serious consideration." That was as far as one could get with that statesman, and evidently the Minister of Public Works is adopting the same method of argument. Here we have a statement from the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) that at one time he applied to the government for a post office in a constitu-

ency which he formerly represented, on the ground that such a building was very much needed. He used all his eloquence and exercised all his influence to have that building put up; it was sorely needed. That is fact number one. Fact number two: The people of that constituency got tired of him and refused to elect him again. Take along with that the next fact, which follows in chronological order. He comes to the government and says, "What I asked you before to do, I ask you now not to do. Do not give this constituency which refuses to express confidence in me the post office which they needed a year ago, and which they still need." I ask the minister again if he subscribes to that doctrine, if that was one of the things that influenced him and his department in refusing justice to this particular place. He has not seen fit to answer that question, and I repeat that until he does answer it he stands in the position of accepting that policy for his department and for the government, namely, that when a Liberal candidate happens to be defeated in a constituency he can come to the government and express his annoyance at the people who defeated him by influencing the government to withhold necessary and just grants to that particular constituency. That is the question, and I say that the minister ought to answer it, and tell us whether that was one of the representations he received that influenced him in cutting this item out of the estimates.

I do not want to be discourteous to my hon. friend in not answering his question, but I thought I had answered it already. He seems to be under the impression that at some time the estimates being prepared by me included an item for a post office at Mahone Bay, and upon that foundation he built up a splendid argument which made me think what an ornament the legal profession lost when the medical profession got my hon. friend. Might I just say in answer to him, and I think this will answer completely both his question and that of my hon. friend from Toronto, that they have both been going on an entirely wrong assumption, because never was there at any time an item for Mahone Bay in either the main or the supplementary estimates prepared by me. So I could never cut the item out. What may have taken place before, I am not in a position to say. I can only say that I certainly would not have cut out from the estimates for political purposes, an item that was already there. I do not think my hon. friend would charge me with that.

Supply-Public Works

I should
like to return the compliment so graciously paid to me by the Minister of Public Works;
I should be lacking in courtesy if I did not do so. He is a brilliant member of the bar, and for him to pay me the compliment of saying that the legal profession lost a bright and shining light when I joined the medical profession I take as a very great compliment indeed, coming from one who is so pre-eminent in the legal profession. It is because of my great and high regard for the hon. Minister of Public Works and for his integrity that I am endeavouring to get him to answer the question, so that he can protect himself against a wrong impression. I confess that I am still in doubt whether or not he or his department was influenced by the efforts of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough, and I do not want to go out of this building to-night with any doubt in regard to that matter.
I do not want to leave here with the impression that he was improperly influenced by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough in not putting this item in the estimates. It does not matter at all whether the item was in the estimates before or since he became Minister of Public Works. The item was in the estimates of the Public Works department, and to that extent the government of the day had recognized the justice of the claims of Mahone Bay, no matter whether the present minister or his predecessor included that item. I am asking the minister if he has been influenced by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough, who says that he influenced somebody.
I did not say that I influenced somebody.

My hon.
friend from Antigonish-Guysborough has stated that he told them not - to put this item in the estimates. Now whom did he tell? He did not tell me. He went to some member of the department and told them, and tried to influence them; and that he was able to influence them is evidenced by the fact that the item has been cut off the estimates, although Mahone Bay was a place that evidently the government had felt should have a post office. Because of my love- for the Minister of Public Works, because of my high eseteem and very great regard for him, and because he is new to the job, I should like him to clear himself of any possible misunderstanding in this matter by getting up and telling the house at once that he was never mfluenced one particle
by the representations made by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough. Immediately he says that, he will rise in the estimation not only of every member on this side, but of every member on the other side as well.

If I wei e of an irascible
temperament I should have a right to feel peeved because, when the hon. Minister of Public Works was paying fhe hon. member for Frontenae the compliment of saying that he would have made a good lawyer, he left me out altogether. Howeeer, I am not of that temperament. I have not for one moment during this debate thought that the influence that was exerted was brought to bear on the present Minister of Public Works. But we have with us to-night his predecessor, and if influence was exerted it must have been upon him, if not upon the present minister. There must be something on the files of the department which will give some explanation of this whole transaction, and I suggest again, Mr. Chairman, that this item be allowed to stand until the minister has had the opportunity of examining his files and bringing down a reasonable explanation of all the circumstances.

The minister stated a while
ago that he did not prepare the estimates last year which included a post office for Mahone Bay. I should like to ask him if he did not bring before the house last session, the supplementary estimates that were not passed the session before, and then ask this house to endorse them, which the house did. I think I am right in that.
The other government did that.
Oh, no.

I remember that last
year our friends opposite complained very much because an item of $12,000 was put in the estimates for a post office at Kensington, Prince Edward Island, and we spent a most interesting evening listening to our friends opposite opposing that item. This year, on the contrary, they do not ask us not to build a post office; they are asking us to build one at Mahone Bay. As we say in French, "autre temps, autres moeurs".
That is what Taschereau says.

We have been
listening for several hours this evening to
Supply-Public Works

hon. gentlemen opposite complaining because the government is not spending $10,000 to build a post office in a place with a population of six or seven hundred.
Twice that.

Even so, I
maintain that hon. members opposite should congratulate and not blame the Minister of Public Works for refusing to spend money on . public buildings in a place of that kind.
It is all right to spend half a million dollars at Washington.

Washington is
going to spend half a million dollars in Ottawa. Is that wrong? I honestly think we should get on with the business of the country. People are anxious that we should not waste money by remaining here longer than necessary, talking about such ridiculous things as the building of a post office at Mahone Ray. We should proceed with the business and pass the vote.

What my hon.
friend from Camrose said about the estimate is quite correct; these estimates were prepared in 1926 with the Mahone Bay item included. The estimates were partly passed in the session of 1926. After the election in the fall of that year, when the present government came back to power, my hon. friend became Minister of Public Works, and the remainder of the estimates of the previous session were brought into this house and passed right here, including the vote for a public building at Mahone Ray.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Without any discussion.

No discussion and no consideration. The present minister was the Minister of Public Works when these items were passed in this house. Now what happened? I had a good deal to do with administering the department during the short time the Meighen government was in power in 1926; and I would say to the hon. minister and to this committee that before the Mahone Bay item was put in the 1926 estimates there would be on the files of the department reports from officers of the department in Nova Scotia as to the necessity of the erection of this public building. Based on that report the then Minister of Public Works put the item in the estimates. The present minister had nothing to do with that, but he was minister when it was put through without discussion in the fall of 1926. Then what happened? When the items for the next year are being prepared the basis on which they 
are first made up is the previous estimates. The Mahone Bay item therefore must have been struck out of the 1927 estimates by somebody; the name would be there unless it had been struck out. There would be some report in the department before the minister would strike out the item, unless he did it entirely of his own volition without reference to the officials of the department. What the members on this side of the house have asked, and quite properly, is that the minister should provide the committee with a copy of the report from the engineer's department on which the item was put in in 1926, also a copy of the report of the officers of the department advising him that the item should be1 struck out in 1927. As I understand the methods of the department that is what happened. There must be a basis, a report or recommendation of some kind, on which the previous minister inserted the item, and there must be something on file in the department on which the present minister based his decision to strike it out in 1927. We ask that that be provided, and I do not think our request is at all unreasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have heard many
theories presented to-night, and I am surprised at the theory suggested by my hon. friend just now. He says the estimates of the year must necessarily be based on the previous year's estimates.
Not necessarily, but usually.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I might remind my hon friend that when he was himself a minister of the crown he was not absolutely faithful in following that theory. He was a prominent member of the government which took office in 1911. I do not know if other members of parliament have had the same experience, but I was a member at the time. There were items in the estimates concerning my own constituency in the session of 1910-11, prior to the election. There was a dissolution of parliament on the reciprocity issue, as my hon. friend remembers.
Very well.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
His leader took office. He was a member of the government, and by some mystery which my hon. friend might explain, these items disappeared. May I add that I did not whine? I took my medicine, and there were many on our side who did likewise for years. An hon. member on the other side made the comment that there are some items for public works in Quebec in these estimates. Maybe Quebec had been deprived

Supply-Public Works
for so long-ten years-that there must be something now in order to repair the loss. But during the whole of the time we were sitting on the opposite side my friends and I took our medicine and did not whine, session after session. But let me say that the estimates are prepared as a new piece of legislation every year. My hon. friend says this item was in the estimates; why did it disappear? It disappeared because the government did not put it back in the estimates. It is asserted that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works is responsible for the estimates. Well, the estimates go before the treasury board and council, and when they leave council they are far different from what they were when my hon. friend brought them in. Last year we had this same discussion and finally the Prime Minister said, in answer to a question which had been repeated as many times as the question has been repeated to-night, that the government was responsible; and the government does take the responsibility. There are questions of policy in that respect as in any other respect. When the estimates are discussed in council the general policy of spending public money for the building of new post offices i3 discussed. Why should we distribute public buildings in Nova Scotia because that province is represented by Conservative members in this house? I cannot see that. It seems to be offered as a reason for the government's erecting buildings there which are not-given to the other provinces. I agree with the leader of the Progressive party when he, says we are wasting the time of the house and the country in discussing Mahone Bay on an item of public works for Nova Scotia. I would ask my hon. friend to accept the very plain and satisfactory explanation which has been given by the Minister of Public Works.

Does the Minister of Justice think the item should have been dropped for the reasons given by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough? We on this side do not claim that public buildings should be erected in Nova Scotia because they are represented by Conservative members; far from it. The minister simply ignores the point at issue. Is the Minister of Public Works or is the government ready to say that this item for Mahone Bay should have been dropped for the reasons given by the member for Antigonish-Guysborough?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It has been dropped
for the reasons whidh have been given by the Minister of Public Works.

He did not give
. any reasons. If the Minister of Justice
says-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He has given the
reason, that it is the policy of t'he government not to build so many public buildings at the present time. We are economizing; we are decreasing the public debt; we are reducing taxation.

I appreciate the attitude
of my hon. friend from Stormont (Mr. Smith). It must surely appear to him to be a waste of time to continue this discussion, but I wish to direct his attention to the fact that the responsibility rests entirely upon the government. The government, through its ministers, has absolutely refused to answer reasonable questions.
No.

Oh yes, I think so. A
very serious principle is involved in the questions which we are putting to the Minister of Public Works and to which we are trying to get answers. Here is an appropriation put in at the desire of a man who was cultivating the constituency.
It was put in by the government.

It was put in by the
government at the request of a man who was cultivating the constituency. I think ne admits that.	.
He says so.
No, I denied it.

I have a great admiration for the frankness of my hon. friend (Mr. Duff). Well, this item is put in because he wants to cultivate that constituency. Then an election js held, and the constituency rejects him; whereupon he comes along and says, "I will get even with you fellows," or something to that effect, and feeling that way he persuades one minister of public works, or another minister of public works, or some person in the department, to strike the item out. He says so himself; there is no doubt about that. Now, what we want is the information from the files of the department giving the reasons for putting that item in and for taking it out. If public business is to be conducted in the open and these appropriations are to be made upon their merits, this question must be answered. We are entitled to an answer, and certainly if there is any resourcefulness on this side of the house we will get the answer.
Supply-Public Works

In answer to
my good friend from Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken), I may say that my understanding of the situation is this. Those votes were in the supplementary estimates. We had a vote for our province in the same estimates. Those estimates lapsed on March 31, and it was necessary to have the votes embodied in the main estimates for last year. My hon. friend will agree with me on that score.
That does not get at the trouble.
I had an estimate for my own county. It would have been dropped the same as the Mahone Bay estimate if I had not kept persistently after the department.
Oh, oh.

Well, the point
I want to make is this:	The hon. member
for Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) failed in his duty -he admitted that last session on the floor of the house-in that he did not press for that vote to be included in the main estimates.
No.

The hon. member cannot
find any statement of mine to that effect; the contrary is the ca<se. I may say that I also have been persistent in my requests since the main estimates were submitted last session.

This is not the
only vote that was dropped from those supplementary estimates; there were hundreds of others, and they were not included in the main estimates. It is up to the member for the constituency to see that the votes he is interested in are so included. It is too late after the main estimates are brought down to complain that his votes are not in. The place to take that matter up is the department, and I think the minister has shown that the vote in question was not included in the main estimates last year along with a great number of others. I notice there was $20,000 voted for Prince Edward Island in 1927-28 which has not been used. We would like to have another post office down there, and I suggest to the minister that this money should be used for the purpose of the erection of a post office building in Alberton in my province.

I should like to ask my
hon. friend (Mr. MacLean) what system he pursued in persuading the Minister of Public Works to look after his constituency; did

he use blarney or the big stick? I happen to be one of those unfortunates who had a vote dropped in the supplementaries, and although I used my best endeavours-and I am Irish too-I was not able to persuade the minister to reinstate that vote in the main estimates last session. But, seriously, Mr. Chairman, I think we have a very important principle to decide. To my mind it is a disgrace to the public life of Canada that a body of men who pose as being capable of administering our national affairs should stoop to the small practice of cutting out a vote for a particular constituency because the electors of that constituency did not see fit to return a member in support of that government. Are we to understand that the people are to be bribed with their own money and that the public works they are granted depends on how they vote? The Minister of Justice gave what he described as a parallel case, but it was not. I take it, Mr.. Chairman, that when those supplementary estimates were brought down in 1926 by the present Minister of Public Works, and he asked this house to endorse them, and they were endorsed, every one of them, those supplementaries should all have been placed in the main estimates for last year to be voted on by this house. It is a different question entirely where you are preparing new estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: I presume that was a change of government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That changes neither
the theory nor the principle.

In this case the government
came in and changed its own estimates. Anyhow, does the minister think that is right?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think a government
must assume responsibility for the estimates which are submitted to the house every session.

Those estimates had been
submitted to, and endorsed by, the house.
By the same minister.

By the same minister, and
yet when the main estimates were brought down the same session certain of those supplementaries had been dropped. I think an explanation is due from the Minister of Public Works.

Supply-Public Works

The Minister of
Public Works has, I think, met the situation fairly and reasonably. But I have some knowledge of the former estimate which is under dispute. We know that during the war years there was a cessation of public works, particularly the erection of post office buildings, throughout the Dominion. We came into power in 1921. We continued that policy, and in 1922, 1923 and 1924 I do not think we were able to prevail upon the treasury board to allow any appropriations in the estimates for the construction of public buildings, although the public service throughout the country demanded such accommodation. No one will deny that during that period the necessity for the construction of these buildings existed. In 1925 I did prevail upon the government to the extent of commencing a small program.
Oh, oh!

Well, that is all
right. A small program was undertaken after I had pointed out to the government that there had been no construction for ten years and that the needs of the country were so great that the government should begin the construction of some public buildings in a small way. As for the selection of the points where these public buildings should be constructed, as the minister in charge at the time I am prepared to take the responsibility. Surely, however, no hon. member will contend that the government, having accepted that policy on the advice of the minister of the day, having voted supply and then having been out of power for a few months and having been returned to office, had not the right to change its policy. The Minister of Public Works may have differed with me there, although I do not say he did; neither do I say that if I had continued in that department I should have been able to prevail upon the ministry to continue that program. I am of the opinion that the public service throughout Canada does require a large expenditure in order that there may be proper accommodation not only for the service but for the employees engaged in it. However, you cannot eat your cake and have it too, and yesterday the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) made statements in this house which I am sure were of great interest to the people of Canada. In fact I am inclined to believe that the judgment of the government was better than mine, and that for the time being the cessation of the construction of public buildings was a wise policy, a policy which has probably been one of the factors which made
it possible for the government to relieve the burden of taxation and to reduce in some degree our enormous public debt.
With regard to what happened in connection with the re-voting of supply after the defeat of the King government in 1926, we know that the incoming government desired to pass these estimates en bloc, and endeavoured to do so. They were not allowed to do that, however, and they carried on during the interval by means of special warrants. When we returned to power it was understood, in order to clear up the financial situation, that it would be wise to vote the supply brought down in the winter of 1926 before the main estimates for last year were brought down.
I do not believe it can be contended that the estimates of this year are to be the basis of the estimates for next year or the year after. Each year is treated by the government with regard to the condition existing at the time the estimates are under consideration, and any one who has served in the ministry knows that the instructions are given out some weeks before the preparation of the estimates is begun.

We do not object so much to the dropping of ,this item as to the reasons given by the hon. member (Mr. Duff) for its disappearance. In order to get on with the work, therefore, may I ask the minister if he will bring down copies of all the reports advising the construction of this building at Mahone Bay, and also copies of the files of record at the time the matter was dropped?

I shall be very glad to produce for the inspection of the committee any files we have with regard to this or any other public building either in or out of the estimates. But in addition to that I want to clear up what I feel to be a misapprehension entertained by the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken) and my hon. friend from Camrose (Mr. Lucas). The estimates to which they were referring were not, as you remember, the estimates that were presented last year; they were the supplementary estimates of the year before, and were presented either in the fall of 1926 or in the early part of the session of 1927. As I said before, no estimates prepared by myself contained the item with reference to Mahone Bay. Those estimates lapsed on March 31. They were not struck out; they went out of existence automatically on account of the ending of the fiscal year. This building at Mahone Bay, and the one to which my hon. friend from Camrose referred, were not reinserted for the reason that the government
Supply-Public Works

considered that other expenditures were more necessary. I want to give my friend an answer which I hope he will consider straight and satisfactory. He asked me as to whether or not I was influenced by the suggestions made by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough. I think he heard my hon. friend state that he had never spoken to me about it, and I have no recollection of his ever having done so. Therefore I am quite sure he is correct when he makes that statement, but at any rate I can say positively that I was not impressed by any such requests. They never came to me, so I could not have been impressed by them.
May I ask the predecessor of my hon. friend whether the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough made representations to him to have that work stopped or struck out of the estimates?

As Minister of
Public Works I found that most of the members came to my office and made quite proper representations in connection with matters pertaining to their districts, and I imagine the hon. member referred to came to my office and made representations similar to those made by other hon. members on both sides of the house.

The explanations which have been given make it more important that the item be allowed to stand until such time as the fife is produced. The minister has stated that the hon. member for Antigonish-Guys-borough did not speak to him in connection with this matter, while the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough positively states that he influenced the minister. That makes it all the more necessary to have the file produced in order to see what method was adopted by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough, and I therefore suggest to the minister (hat this item be allowed to stand until the file is produced.

I have already stated to my hon. friend that I have no objection to producing the file, and I think my hon. friend should take my word for it. I say the file will be produced, and whatever correspondence took place will be laid on the table. On that undertaking I think my hon. friends might see their way clear to allow the item to pass.
A moment ago the minister said he would not produce the files of anything except the items in the present estimates.
No, no.
Do I understand the minister to say now that the file having to do with this particular matter will be produced?
Yes.
Then I presume the minister will allow the item to stand.
Carried.
Let the item stand. We may get information about it which will alter our view.
I call the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that that file has no reference to, or no bearing upon, the items under discussion.
But the items under discussion offer us the only opportunity we shall have of discussing the matter.
No, no.
I think so. I submit that we ought to have the information we are asking for before this item is disposed of.

If the minister will provide the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg with the files that refer to Mahone Bay, and allow him to discuss the matter on "harbours and rivers, Nova Scotia", if he chooses to do so, will that be satisfactory?
Quite satisfactory.
Then the minister will give us the assurance that the hon. member (Mr. Ernst) can discuss the Mahone Bay matter, when he has the papers, under the item: "harbours and rivers, Nova Scotia"?
Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Another night of it!

I must confess that I am still not satisfied, because when the vote for harbours and rivers is up it may mot be possible for me to be present. Therefore I will ask the minister to allow this item to stand until such time as the file is here.
No, mo.

I should hate to have to talk until 11 o'clock in order to explain my position. The Minister of Public Health (Mr. King) has advanced contentions which in reality are not arguments at all and have nothing to do with the question at issue. We n.ow get back to the basic issue, which is that the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough has stated that he did certain things; he had a certain vote put in the estimates and afterwards had that vote taken out. He has stated

Supply-Public Works
that two years in succession. Now what possible objection can there be to allowing the item to stand and then producing the file containing the papers referring to this matter, so that we can discuss it at a future date?

I submit that this is a request which has frequently been made in this committee and agreed to. You do not make any progress by simply crowding an item through. I am sure I am right in stating that neither the minister nor any member of the government has the slightest intention of preventing further discussion of this matter, and where can the discussion more appropriately take place than under this item? Let the item stand, as has been done hundreds of times in my experience. Whenever there was a decided difference of opinion, or when members have asked that certain items should stand until further information is forthcoming, the request has been acceded to no matter what government was in power. Why should my hon. friend object to such a procedure? If the government has confidence in the honesty of these items it should be the first to meet that request and say "very well; let us get on with the business; we will take up something else, and when you have had an opportunity to look into this matter we will resume the discussion." My hon. friends are not losing any time by following this course, but they cannot crowd an item through in the face of general opposition.

"Crowd"?
Mr. EDWARD'S (Frontenac): If the government persists in its course I cannot use any other word. Why not let this item stand and go ahead with other items?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Is there any objection to the items in question? Has any information been asked for in regard to them?
Yes.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Not a bit.

Excuse me, but I am afraid my hon. friend and I do not see this matter in exactly the same light. I endeavoured to put myself straight by asking the chairman a question some time ago. If I understood him correctly, and I think I did, he considered the discussion was perfectly proper. I understood the government also considered it proper. I understood it was permissible to discuss public buildings under this vote, even though certain public buildings may not be mentioned in it, and I think that is the proper course to pursue. We shall not be doing wrong if we follow the general principle that where there is a decided difference of opinion, and further information is asked for, we allow the item to stand, as has been done hundreds of times in this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would agree with my hon. friend if the item in question was for Mahone Bay, but there is nothing concerning that place in this item. The items here relate to Halifax, North Sydney and Truro. Item 125 deals with Dominion public buildings generally. There *is where the whole discussion should properly have taken place, as was stated by the chairman. Why not wait until that item is reached, if you deem it necessary to renew the discussion, and then you will have the file promised by the Minister of Public Works.

I appreciate the point of the Minister of Justice, but under our constitutional system when a government comes to the house and asks for supply, it is the right of any member to bring any grievance to the notice of parliament, and to ask for redress before any money is voted. That is the democratic principle of our British institutions, and it is one which has always been recognized. I recognize my hon. friend's point that the discussion might be taken up under item 125, but I maintain nevertheless that the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg has a right to make representations with respect to any grievance before supply is granted on any item.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I would
agree with the hon. member if any question were raised with respect to any item in this vote. But inasmuch as no question has been raised nor any information demanded regarding any items enumerated in the vote, it seems a strange thing for hon. gentlemen to ask that the whole vote should stand when they can discuss the matter later in the light of the information contained in the papers to be brought down. The request of my hon. friend does not exhibit any desire to expedite public business.

May I ask my hon. friend one question: Does 'he not recognize the soundness of the principle that any member representing the people has a right to make representations with respect to a grievance and to have that grievance rectified by parliament, or by the government, before any supplies whatever are granted?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
That right is not being denied. The hon. gentleman is right when he says that items are allowed to stand with respect to which information is
Supply-Public Works

desired. But no information is sought with respect to the vote under consideration, and a promise has been given to the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg that as regards the item he has in mind the information will be brought down and he will be given an opportunity to discuss it. I fail to understand therefore why this particular item should stand.

One word in reply to the
Minister of the Interior. He seems to have overlooked the fact-possibly he was not here during the whole discussion-that there are two aspects to this question. There is the aspect of the vote for the post office at Mahone Bay which was dropped last year from the main estimates that were tabled. There is also the question of the principle as affecting the estimates under consideration and other estimates. Certain representations were made by the hon. member for Ant.igon-ish-Guysborough, representations as to the principle upon which votes got into the estimates and were taken out. Before any estimate passes the house it is really the privilege of the house to know whether or not that principle governs in the voting of public money. That is really the question at issue apart altogether from the question of Mahone Bay. And that is why I ask that the vote stand.

My hon. friend will admit that the principle can be discussed on any vote which comes before the house on any occasion. The right to discuss that principle is inalienable; any member can invoke it on any vote which comes up. There is therefore no reason why this particular vote should be held up, for it does not touch the principle just enunciated by my hon. friend any more than does any other vote. In view of the fact that the Minister of Public Works has promised to bring down the papers I submit that the item should be allowed to pass. The minister's word is good when he promises, although I admit he is the hardest man to get to make a promise. However, he has definitely promised to bring down the papers with respect to this matter, and so far as the general principle is concerned it can, I say, be discussed on any vote. It is not correct to say that any gentleman is being denied the right to air a grievance affecting a matter of principle. I urge my hon. friend, on the very ground he himself takes with regard to the principle at stake, to allow the item under discussion to pass on the understanding that he may discuss that principle later. He may discuss it not once but one hundred times if he wishes to do so; there can be no difficulty about that. Other-
wise he must take the responsibility for merely obstructing until eleven o'clock, and that I do not think is desired. Surely this meets my hon. friend at all points. The hon member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley). who is leading the opposition at the moment, suggested the course I am urging, and if we adopt it we can make some progress, at the same time giving the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg every opportunity on another occasion to discuss both the principle and the specific matter relating to Mahone Bay.

It is not my purpose to
obstruct, and I appreciate the honeyed words of the Minister of Railways. But the assurance which he gives is somewhat broader than that suggested by the hon. member for Argenteuil and accepted by the Minister of Public Works. If the Minister of Public Works will assure me that on some other vote I may discuss not only the principle but the particular question with reference to the post office, I am content. I am not discussing the matter merely for the sake of obstruction.

My hon. friend said something about not being able to be here during the discussion of the vote for harbours and rivers. If he is not here when item 125 is discussed I will undertake to hold some other item to enable him to bring the matter up. He might let the item pass now,
That is perfectly satisfactory.

Any arrangement as to
the Mahohe Bay matter reached by or between the minister and any member on this side does not interest me in the slightest. My well-beloved and usually generous friend, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), made some reference to the granting of post offices to constituencies represented by Conservatives. I am not asking for a post office and I have not done so. What I am asking for is to have repairs and alterations made to a building which is about fifty years old, the necessity for the repairs and alterations is admitted by the department, having been a matter of knowledge to them for several years. The request has been supported by the gentleman who opposed me in the county of Pictou, and correspondence from him is on file in the department in which he urges the importance of the work. I obtained from the minister last year what I consider a gentleman's agreement and I do not now propose to be put off without a definite assurance that something will be done in the matter within a reasonable time.

Supply-Public Works

I have deferred discussing the question I am now going to bring up until the matter of the Mahone Bay post office should have been settled or an answer given by the minister. Since we have failed to secure any satisfactory reply in that regard I wish now to refer to the item of $1,300 for the tractor for postal purposes at Truro. I shall ask the minister a question which I am sure it is within his power to answer. But before doing so I want to take up the reference which the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) has made to my remarks concerning the purchase of a certain lot in Truro. In Hansard of February 15 the following questions and answers are given:
Truro Post Office Site
Mr. MacNutt:
1.	On what date was a lot in the town of Truro, Nova Scotia, purchased for a new post office site?
2.	What price was paid for said lot?
3.	To whom was said lot sold?
4.	What proportion, if any, of original lot was sold for church building purposes?
5.	Who was purchaser of remaining portion of lot?
6.	What price was paid by each of the two buyers ?
Mr. Mackenzie King (for the Minister of Public Works):
1.	July 11, 1914.
2.	$17,000.
3.	Part of site (100 feet by 165 feet) to St. James Presbyterian church for $3,300 and remainder of site (124 feet by 165 feet) to G-eo. L. Brenton for $4,500.
4.	5 and 6. Answered by No .3.
Now the committee will see that a very valuable lot in Truro, for some reason or other, was sold at a loss to the country of almost $10,000.

Was it ever worth what
was paid for it originally?

At the time these lots
were bought real estate values were higher than at present.

In 1914. In that town
prices were then high and this price was not considered exorbitant.

From whom was it
bought originally?

I did not ask that question, but I understand that it was bought from a widow. I know that in the town in which I live, Stewiacke, a lot was purchased for a post office from the widow of one of the strongest Liberals there.

Is that the same lot?
56103-39	'

No. In the town of
Stewiacke to-day we are carrying on our post office business in a little ten-by-twelve office which is utterly unfit for the purpose. I hope the minister will not decide to dispose of that lot, which was bought in 1914, in the same way that the department did in the case of the lot in Truro. In view of the report from the architects of the department, to the effect that the building at Truro could not possibly be remodelled except at an enormous cost, almost equal to the amount that would furnish a new building, I should like to know from the minister upon whose recommendation the department has acted. The people of the town of Truro feel this very keenly. They feel that they have received a black eye by having this lot disposed of at the price which the department realized. I hope the minister has the information available so that he can give it to us to-night.

I should like to be allowed
to say a word in regard to the Truro situation in reply to what the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. MacNutt) has just said. In December, 1926, at the request of the board of trade of the town of Truro, I visited that town. I arrived at nine o'clock in the morning, on my way from New Glasgow to Moncton, and met the members of the board of trade and some members of the city council. I went down with them, examined both properties thoroughly, and made a thorough examination of the present post office accommodation. At their suggestion, as Postmaster General, I recommended to the Department of Public Works that the lot purchased in 1914 between the two churches be disposed of because according to their opinion, in agreement with my own, there was sufficient real estate attached to the present building at Truro to add all the modern improvements necessary to give Truro all the postal and customs accommodation it would. need for the next twenty years. I had the chairman, the secretary, and other members of the board of trade with me, and we fully discussed the matter. We returned to the station awaiting the train I was to take, and there it was decided that I should recommend to the Minister of Public Works the sale of the property thrrt had been bought in 1914, and recommend also the necessary improvements to the present building along modem lines. The present building can be improved, and a modem up-to-date addition can be made to it on a property the rear of which is vacant to-day, sufficient to give the town of Truro all the postal and customs accommodation that it will need for the next

Supply-Public Works

twenty years, without having to build a new building on a new site. More than that, the site of the present post office at Truro is the best available site in the whole town. It is more centrally located than the property that was purchased between the two churches at Truro, and I might add that there was a decided objection from the adherents of both churches that a public building should be put up in between the two churches. There is the history of my investigation as Postmaster General of the conditions at Truro, and it was upon my recommendation as Postmaster General that this property was disposed of. But before I took that action, I received the recommendation of the members of the board of trade at Truro, who met me at the station and visited both sites with me.

I am very glad to have the minister acknowledge that he is responsible for the sale of the lot in the town of Truro. I am receiving letters frequently, and recently almost daily, asking me to have this matter brought up in the house, and these letters are not all from Conservatives either. I would like to know the gentlemen who accompanied the minister on that occasion.
The chairman of the board of trade was one, and the secretary of the board of trade was another.

Evidently a change has come over the people since, from the information I am receiving. I am very glad, however, that the onus of the sale of this lot in the town of Truro is now placed upon the shoulders of the Postmaster General.
And upon the members of the board of trade of Truro. They recommended it.

I will allow them to speak for themselves. I think I would take the opinion and the judgment of such men as the architect to whom I referred earlier in the evening, Mr. Rankin, who spent several days in that town making a report on the old post office, rather than the report of the Postmaster General, notwithstanding the high opinion I hold of his judgment. I think there is not a member of this house on either side who has ever made an attempt to remodel an old building, and this building is forty-four years old, who did not regret before he got through that he had ever started. The report I have referred to, which is on file in the Public Works department, shows that the cost of remodelling the old building to put it in the condition the public service requires would be almost equal to the cost of a new building, and even then you would still have [Mr. Veniot.l
an old building. I need not refer to the condition of the present building. The minister says that there is a lot of room in the rear. We know that there is room at the rear in nearly all our public buildings, but I say that the building will be entirely inadequate when it is completed and the cost will be so great that it would almost build a new one. I appeal to the Minister of Public Works, before attempting to spend a large amount of money on the Truro post office, to go very carefully and take the advice of his architects, who have already reported on it.
I vrould aek the minister to give some explanation of these different items.

Perhaps my bon. friend
was not in earlier in the evening when I gave an explanation.
Yes, I was.

The first $25,000 is a payment to the Department of Railways and Canals for accommodation. It is really in the nature of a rental agreement. It is the amount that after considerable negotiation was arrived at as a fair price.

What accommodation
was secured?

It is the immigration
building. We were able to arrive at that arrangement with the Department of Railways and Canals. This is the amount we paid last year, and for some years past I think. The item of $45,000 is required for repairs to buildings and wharves at the Royal Canadian Naval barracks. These are rather extensive repairs. First, there are general repairs to wharves and cambers, $20,000; reconstruction of foundation of thirty-ton crane, and erection of crane, $15,000; repairs and construction of parade and recreation ground, $10,000, or a total of $45,000. The next item of $5,700 is required for repairs and improvements to Rockhead hospital. This has been requested by the Department of Health. The alterations asked fpr consist of installing door bells, electric fixtures, and other items, eighteen altogether. The next item is $7,500 for an addition to a public building in North Sydney. If my recollection serves me aright, that is for customs purposes. It is a one storey building at the rear of a public building, and it is necessitated very largely on account of the seizures of liquor. They already have so many seizures on hand that their accommodation is practically all taken up.

Is it not a fact that seized liquor is immediately destroyed?

Supply-Public Works
No.
What is done with it?
It is kept for thirty days before it is destroyed.
It is consumed.
Who consumes it? According to the Postmaster General the building is needed to hold the liquor for thirty days so that it can be poured down the sewer.
I did not say it was poured down the sewer; I said it was destroyed.
Did the hon. member not say something about thirty days?
Yes.

According to this other
minister the building is required to hold liquor for thirty days so that it can then be destroyed. If that is the only use for the building the government had better make a change in the law, save the $7,500 and destroy the liquor at once.

This addition was asked for by the Commissioner of Customs in a letter dated the 18th of November, as follows:
I have to request that a one-storey brick building 30 feet x 70 feet be erected at the rear of the North Sydney, N.S., public building in order to provide adequate facilities for the examination of importations and more especially for the safe custody of seized goods.
This accommodation is absolutely necessary, as North Sydney is the headquarters for our preventive service operations around Cape Breton island and it is impossible to obtain the required security in rented premises. Alcoholic liquors constitute the bulk of the seizures, and the goods have to be retained for long periods on account of actions pending in the courts.
Quite satisfactory.
As a matter of information regarding the naval barracks, did the minister state how many men are retained there on service or kept in the barracks?
The request made for this accommodation does not, I regret to say, state the number of men.
Is it used now as a barracks, or is it in preparation for a new navy?

This is an item which has been passed for a good many years. The amount is generally $30,000. Last year, however, there was no vote at all, and the additional $15,000 is on account of the repairs required.
I should like to know what corps is being held in those barracks.
I cannot tell the number of men,-probably about 200. The naval stations are situated at Halifax and Esquimau.
Is this $25,000 for the accommodation of immigrants? Can the minister tell me how many immigrants came into Halifax last year?

I am afraid my hon. friend will have to ask the Minister of Immigration that question. This is the amount of the rental for the immigration halls at that point. As I said before it has been paid for a number of years. Formerly there was an arrangement by which the departments divided the expense in a certain way, and it did not work out satisfactorily. After considerable negotiation an arrangement was made for a lump sum of $25,000 to be paid by the one department to the other.

Item agreed to.
Public buildings, New Brunswick-St. John quarantine station, Partridge Island-repairs and improvements, $13,600.

Will the
minister give me some information as to the details of this vote?

This amount is required
for general repairs and improvements to St. John quarantine station as requested by the Department of Public Health through the deputy minister in a communication dated December 2, 1927. The memorandum is as follows:
The proposed works consist of a large number of small miscellaneous items which are estimated to cost $13,520. They are as follows:
Alterations and repairs:
(1) Power House:
Cut out defective bricks in external walls and replace with new and coat walls externally with three coats minwax.
Construct one new store for bunkering coal, in location to be decided between Public Works department resident architect and medical superintendent.
Provide six ladders for fighting fire which may occur in the various buildings, (twenty feet to thirty feet long).
Cut opening between boiler room and main hall 2 ft x 3 ft for ventilating and heating purposes, provided with trims complete.
And other similar details which I shall be glad to read if my hon. friend desires them.

May I ask the minister if there is any special condition about New Brunswick to account for the presence of only-one item in the estimates for the province- $13,600 for the St. John quarantine station? There is no epidemic in the province so far as: I know. Why therefore this special and sole attention to the quarantine station? It is
Supply-Public Works

unfortunate if the quarantine station has the effect of keeping out of the province all votes for public buildings.

Do I understand my hon. friend to object to the vote?
Mr. MaeLAREN: Yes, I am objecting to the smallness of the vote.
I can assure my hon. friend that the vote is adequate to make the required improvements in the economical manner in which we make them.

Mr. Chairman, I have been very much amused by the defence offered by the government to-night of public expenditures, particularly those in the maritime provinces. Especially amusing was the explanation given by the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) of the extensions to be made at the Truro post office. It is becoming, a habit with the government to fit up old buildings as best they can, jack them up, piaster and replaster them, leaving them in an unsanitary condition, in those constituencies where the Liberal candidate was not successful at the last election. In 1885 a post office was constructed in the city of Moncton when the population was about five thousand. That building has been condemned from time to time by the architect of the Public Works department, by the architect of the Po3t Office department and by every other official who has inspected it. Yet the gross postal receipts have increased from $65,000 to over $400,000 a year, with net receipts of over $300,000, standing I think about sixth in the whole Dominion in so far as revenue is concerned.
A few moments ago members of the government referred to orders in council, and the former Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) stated that having been out of power for something like two months, the items they had placed in the estimates had no effect whatever on their being returned to power again. That is a very weak argument, and I think no one realizes it better than the hon. gentleman himself. However, he put it over in very good shape.
The discussion on the Mahone Bay post office vote discloses the fact that a defeated and disappointed Liberal candidate was able to prevail on the minister to withdraw that vote for what was admittedly a public necessity. If that is what this government is ready to do on the recommendation of a discredited candidate, which means that they are prepared to accept the responsibility of withholding from the general public in any constituency a post office or any other necessary public building, then I say the time will come when the electorate will deal with that government.

In the city of Moncton a private individual, a supporter of the present administration, purchased a property for something like $17,000. Four or five years ago, possibly six, but I think no more, the government, having been impressed with the necessity of building a post office in that city, selected t(he very property that this gentleman had purchased. An election was in sight, and I presume it was thought proper to pay a respectable price to the owner, and they handed him $49,000. This property they rented afterwards at $40 a month, and to-day it is occupied by an employee of the Canadian National Railways at a rental of no more than $49 per month, the government paying the taxes-a very fine income from an investment of nearly $50,000.
Now, from time to time the government has promised the people of Moncton a post office. As a matter of fact the present building is not sanitary, and it is so inadequate that the government has found it necessary to go to a middleman and get him to rent a place across the street and sublet it to the department. That is the condition of affairs there to-day-the government instead of renting the property from the owner is renting it from a middleman.
Not for the post office.

That is the practice of this
government. As I say, the people of Moncton require a new post office building. The old building has been repaired from time to time, and instead of putting up a new post office- which, as I have shown, is very badly needed to carry on properly the business of the department-the government are subjecting the postal employees to the inconvenience of looking after the public business in a building which has been condemned and which is inadequate and badly located.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Monday, February 20, 1928
